As for those with outflows, they are further the defiled dharmas and so forth described by the faction of darkness (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
Regarding the dharmas such as the "white friend" and so forth, these are the various pure dharmas and so on.

Within this, whether the mind possesses reality or lacks reality—these two constitute that which accords with those dharmas, wherein there are wholesome and unwholesome states, up to and including those with outflows and those without outflows.
That all these two extremes are unattainable, inexpressible, and indefinable is called the true and correct contemplation of the Middle Way among all phenomena.
Within this, they are "unattainable" because of that [erroneous] view.
That which is "inexpressible" is so called solely because it refers to that [reality].
Its essence is inexpressible; thus, when others come to inquire, one cannot provide a definitive explanation.
Furthermore, there is another secondary meaning:
It should be understood that "wholesome and unwholesome" constitutes the fundamental basis, while the subsequent successive phrases provide the correct explanation.
Having already explained the meaning of the Middle Way as an antidote to the non-Buddhists and Śrāvakas, he now explains the side of the Bodhisattvas as an antidote.
Regarding the antidote to this, it is said that the perverted grasping at a permanent self held by various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) arises from what?
It is said to be like a blind person falling to the ground.

Because the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas practice the vision of the selflessness of persons and have already awakened only to the functioning of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), they give rise to [the realization of] the impermanence and selflessness of all conditioned phenomena.

Furthermore, regarding the fundamental insight into the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), it arises from the understanding that all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and selfless.
When a Bodhisattva perceives and practices this selflessness of phenomena, they have already fundamentally cultivated the selflessness of phenomena.

Subsequently, because there are three kinds of transverse attachments to extremes, [the Buddha] manifests the counteractive measures for these transverse attachments to self-characteristics, speaking of them in relation to matters of existence and non-existence.

“Kāśyapa! ‘Existence’ is one extreme; ‘non-existence’ is the second extreme. Even up to ‘no life, no consciousness, no sensation, and no attachment’—this is called the Middle Way, the true and correct contemplation of all phenomena.”
As it is said, one should understand that based on the antidote to obscuration, what is clung to as ignorance is spoken of as clarity.
The Sūtra states: "Kāśyapa!

For your sake I have taught the twelve links of dependent origination, namely: ignorance conditions volitional formations, and so on, until: with the cessation of ignorance, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and delusion cease."

Because one clings to the conditioned and the unconditioned, as well as to cessation and other paths, there arise such phrases as "activity" and "cessation of activity. The remedies for these various forms of clinging are called "non-duality."
Because it is free from the nature of conceptual construction and discrimination, it is the nature of equality.

Since it is taught as having the characteristic of non-duality, it is not that clear wisdom (*vidyā*) can produce it, nor that ignorance (*avidyā*) can extinguish it; it is not that formative factors (*saṃskāra*) and so forth can eliminate it, nor that its extinction can be attained. Thus, although the characteristics of the nature of conceptual construction are established, [it remains thus].
Regarding all such wisdom as this, it is capable of preventing the extreme of slander.

When it is said that "it is neither clarity nor ignorance," and so forth—if one does not make all phenomena empty by means of emptiness, but rather the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is itself empty; if one does not make all phenomena signless by means of the signless, but rather phenomena themselves are signless; and so on, up to the point that phenomena themselves are without arising, without grasping, and without intrinsic nature—what meaning is being demonstrated?

Having already attained the understanding that the characteristics such as clarity and emptiness are of the nature of conceptual discrimination regarding phenomena produced by causes and conditions, or of the nature of fulfillment, one cannot cause them to become empty. Why is this?
Such is the nature of all phenomena.

Whether by way of their imagined and discriminated nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) or their perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), all phenomena are empty; thus it extends even to the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

This teaching of "having clarity" and "having those obscurations" demonstrates the nature of perfection (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) as being free from conceptual construction; it serves to prevent and protect against the extreme of nihilistic denial by means of seven kinds of antidotes to obscurations within this context. Thus, clarity is explained as emptiness, up to the point where the seven kinds of obscurations are shown to be non-existent in nature.
First, regarding "view," emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is taught as its antidote;
regarding the characteristics of greed, hatred, and delusion which act as causes, the signless (*animitta*) is taught as their antidote;
and regarding the grasping for aspirations within existence, the wishless (*apraṇihita*) is taught as its antidote.
Furthermore, there are various karmic formations that are created; to counteract these, "non-action" is taught.
Because those [formations] have results, there is birth; to counteract this, "non-birth" is taught.
Once born, suffering and pleasure necessarily arise; to counteract this, "non-arising" is taught.
Because one perceives emptiness, the conceit "I am" arises; to counteract this, it is taught that all phenomena likewise lack intrinsic nature.
Within this context, one practices the contemplation of non-self to prevent the grasping at the characteristics of a person.

Regarding the remaining characteristics, such as non-duality and so forth: because all phenomena are characterized by grasping, Kāśyapa, it is said that it is not that there are no persons; therefore, it is called "emptiness."
"Emptiness is empty of itself" means that it negates the arbitrary grasping at signs regarding persons and phenomena; it does not mean the extinction of sentient beings' grasping at signs.

One cultivates emptiness not for the sake of extinguishing sentient beings' grasping at signs, but because emptiness is empty of itself, thereby demonstrating the extinction of signs within phenomena.

Because emptiness is empty by virtue of being a nature falsely grasped through conceptual discrimination, how much more so are all phenomena false? This is because they are what is grasped within conceptual discrimination.
Thus, emptiness is not a functional entity, for it does not exist within the nature falsely grasped through conceptual discrimination.
Furthermore, it is not that there is no basis, for it exists within the nature of accomplishment (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Just as with space, so too are all phenomena; because of grasping at phenomena, the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is demonstrated.
However, that [is so] because it is accomplished through manifestation.
Regarding the sun and moon, the Sūtra states: "The past limit is empty, the middle limit is empty, and the future limit is also empty," thereby manifesting [their presence] at all times.
Because the bodies of ordinary beings, those in training (*śaikṣa*), and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are manifested therein.
When it is said, "You should rely upon emptiness," it is because you must rely on the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Regarding the manifestation within emptiness as a skillful means for protection, do not rely on the person; rely instead on the definitive meaning.
Having refuted that [basis], it is called "abiding in the basis of the definitive meaning.
This is because all human conceptualization and its causal factors consist of those two types of *pudgala*.
As for the statement, "If one attains emptiness, one then relies upon emptiness," what meaning does this demonstrate?
Because one awakens to emptiness through non-conceptualization, one should rely upon the meaning of emptiness.
Having thus relied [upon it], since one previously clung to the view of a personal self and harbored grasping attachments, both the self and phenomena are lost, causing them to be swiftly discarded.
Because this explains and establishes [the teaching] by means of both performing that [action] and recognizing the rapid loss [of merit], it says: "Kāśyapa!
It is better to give rise to a view of self as large as Mount Sumeru than a view of emptiness; for all views can only be extinguished by emptiness."

Because one realizes emptiness through discriminative awareness, one understands the true meaning of the emptiness of the conceit of self (*asmimāna*), such that it cannot be grasped; yet to give rise to slander against this realization for the sake of attaining it is even more difficult, as it involves the removal of the view of a person (*pudgaladṛṣṭi*).
If your medicine stirs the illness within but it does not emerge, this is called "having an illness.
As the Sūtra says: "Kāśyapa!..."
"If one gives rise to the view of emptiness, I say that such a person is incurable.
Or, by means of false attachment and conceptualization, they arbitrarily grasp at the meaning that all things and all non-things [are empty], despite these being merely conventional designations.
The analogy of space refers to the protection against the distorted apprehension of transformation.
If there is the view of emptiness, because of that emptiness, one seeks non-existence within phenomena such as form;
thus, one makes a conceptual distinction of non-existence regarding what is existent. This is called the arbitrary apprehension within that transformation.

These phenomena such as form and so forth are by their very nature devoid of analogy; yet, if one gives rise to the seeking to eliminate them for the sake of all sentient beings, this is an analogy for practice.
Within the essence of emptiness, one is deludedly discriminating against that essence out of fear of it, as if it were an illusion.
If phenomena such as form did not exist, the cultivation of various practices would be in vain; it is to guard against this affliction that the analogy of the painter is taught.
Just as if there were no actual ghost, the painter, having himself engaged in conceptual discrimination and deliberation, becomes deluded and falls prostrate to the ground.

In this way, although there are no such entities as form and so forth, because ordinary worldlings falsely engage in conceptualization and mental activity, the wheel of the world continues to turn; therefore, in order to eliminate that ignorance, spiritual practice is not in vain.
The previous section has already explained the activity of deluded discrimination; now, it explains the non-illusory matters within the activity of undertaking practice.
If this were merely a deluded mind, how could that mind be capable of cognition?
Because that mind is difficult to restrain and protect, it was said previously that one must first prevent the arising of false conceptualizations and grasping.
Now, since it is necessary to prevent the occurrence of the activity of issuing forth [conceptualization], the analogy of a magician is given.
In this context, "abiding like a magician" refers to the wisdom of focused mindfulness.
"Performing illusions like a magician" refers to the wisdom that observes the absence of phenomena.

"Like one who eats" refers solely to the wisdom that observes the absence of conceptual thought; because it observes things as being like space and so forth, and because it is fundamentally seen through the faculty of noble wisdom as it truly is, [phenomena] do not exist.
How can one attain supramundane knowledge through observation that is not in accordance with reality?
To preclude such an objection, it is said that by means of the friction of two pieces of wood, one attains it through the condition of meditative reflection in a state of seclusion.
The noble faculty of wisdom arises from the locus of fire; having arisen, it abandons that [fire] and enters tranquil contemplation—this should be understood as a manifestation.
Is this for the sake of counteracting existing ignorance with wisdom, or for the sake of preventing what has not yet arisen?
Therefore, the analogy of the lamp’s light is taught.
Wisdom has no conceptual characteristics; it is shown that at the very moment wisdom arises, it acts as the antidote to ignorance.
How can there be an antidote that begins at a specific point for afflictions and defilements that have no beginning?
Because it can extinguish and prevent difficulties, the metaphor of the "inner lamp" is taught.
This metaphor illustrates the meaning of the Middle Way; it is explained here in brief.
For a detailed analysis, one should understand that it differs according to the bodhisattva’s abiding in the morality of correct practice (*samyakpratipatti-śīla*).

A Bodhisattva who practices the Dharma speaks of the principles of conventional truth and the analytical exposition of ultimate truth; he manifests gradual teaching rather than grasping at sounds as they are heard.
Because of such characteristics, he does not rely upon the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Having encountered them, he speaks of those who have previously made offerings and cultivated roots of goodness therein; these are those who incline toward the profound dharmas of the Mahāyāna and accord with emptiness, as they are subsumed within the principle of the ultimate truth through both conceptualization and non-conceptualization.

That which is taught regarding the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is spoken solely within the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the single *dharmadhātu*.

For this reason, that which accords with and inclines toward the basis is called "tranquility of practice" (*caryā-śānti*); because it is tranquility of practice, it is termed the meaning of "inclining toward the Middle Way."

Thus, having refuted those [erroneous] views, he explains the thirteen aspects of the Middle Way: explaining the emptiness of sentient beings as the selflessness of sentient beings, and the emptiness of phenomena as the selflessness of phenomena.
Transverse discrimination consists of [the views of] extremes and the denial of those extremes, as well as the realization of the Dharma and the aspiration directed toward great enlightenment.
Having practiced in this way, one feels no weariness or satiety amidst afflictions and suffering, and possesses superior faith in the two kinds of selflessness.
In the absence of a self before, the absence of a self after is the ultimate exhaustion that reaches all emptinesses; this is likewise explained as the manifestation of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).
How is the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*) explained?
Because it is characterized by a single mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*).
To say "if one does not observe for oneself" is to demonstrate a lack of self-awareness; herein lies this non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*).

There are three kinds of non-conceptual matters: regarding the phenomena of sentient beings, it clarifies the matter of the aggregates (*skandha*) and their various aspects; it further clarifies, within the various elements (*dhātu*), the matter of their experiential enjoyment, such as the sense bases (*āyatana*), both internally, externally, and in the intermediate state between the two, just as ordinary people falsely cling to them.

If one does not perceive a self, how can one explain the realization of the selflessness of persons? It is because [the Buddha] manifests this through awakening to a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*).

Since there is this matter of awakening within it, he says that one should not contemplate [it] as permanent; for one knows that what returns to those three types of objects is the permanence imagined and grasped by ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*), since one does not perceive the distinct characteristics of a self as imagined by ordinary people.
Regarding impermanent phenomena such as the aggregates (*skandha*), how is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) explained?
It is shown that this is because they are not awakened to by means of even a single characteristic.

This is because it is taught that they are not to be viewed as impermanent; thus one knows that within these [phenomena] there exists this matter of non-awakening. Because one returns to the impermanent course within those very phenomena, the internal, external, and the two intermediates are merely conventional designations based on the false attachments of ordinary beings; their essential nature cannot be perceived.

Once one has attained the realization of impermanence yet still clings to it, one arbitrarily imposes [conceptual constructs] upon that which is ineffable; how, then, can one explain the teaching of the selflessness of phenomena?
It is shown by means of awakening to the single characteristic.

Because there is this cognition therein that cognizes an object, one returns to that very object as the realm of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) which is cognized and perceived; it is realized only through internal personal realization (*pratyātma-adhigama*), and cannot be described by others.
That [nature] has six characteristics; it is unlike the nature as it is conceptually grasped, falsely perceived, and verbally described by ordinary people.
What are these six?
That which is non-material cannot be identified or pointed out by oneself, nor can it be said to be "this."
This is that which is invisible; therefore, it cannot be apprehended.
It is shown to others as non-abiding because it transcends the sphere of the sensory faculties (*indriya*), for in that place, the sense-faculties such as form (*rūpa*) cannot abide.
It is signless because it is free from the nature and characteristics of conceptual thought.
It is indeterminate because it is beyond the sphere of the mental consciousness.
It is unattached because it is devoid of the activity of afflictions.
How is the erroneous conceptualization of existence as having limits established and explained?
It is because two kinds of superior characteristics are demonstrated through correct exposition, and because their essential nature and characteristics are demonstrated through correct exposition.
Among these, what is the superior and correct teaching regarding nature and characteristics?
One should know that there are eight types of higher and higher [views].
Within those very matters, there is the constant correct adherence to permanence and the correct adherence to impermanence.
Furthermore, based on the correct adherence to permanence, there is the correct adherence to the grasping at a self;
based on the adherence to impermanence, there is the adherence to non-self;
and based on the grasping adherence to non-self, there is the great adherence to the grasping at a real mind.
Based on the existence of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), it is said that one does not grasp at a real mind.
One seeks that which is its basis, and further seeks that which seeks it; based upon grasping and based upon the common conformity to grasping, one grasps an unreal mind.
Regarding the attachment to what is grasped as unwholesome and so forth, up to the grasping of the signs of defiled attachment, there are five kinds of obstacles and afflictions.
Within these defiled phenomena, there are the afflictions of perversion, denial, arousal, coarseness, and impermanence, based on the mind that grasps at reality.

As for their antidotes, within pure phenomena, there is the establishment of the wholesome and so forth, up to the establishment of pure attainment; these constitute the eight kinds of supreme establishments.
Because the bodhisattva does not perceive, recollect, or follow after them, nor does he cling to them, these eight kinds of supreme establishments [are established].
It is not taught as conformity because it does not encourage others;
it is not awakened to as conformity because it does not move others.

Regarding "the attachment to peace based on reality therein": this clarifies that within these eight kinds of superior objects of peace, ordinary beings fixate their attention upon them and practice attachment to peace through the nature of provisional usage.
Regarding the statement that there is such an "establishment," how does it refute the extreme of nihilism?
It is because of this single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) that the existence of the object of nihilistic denial is demonstrated.

Within this, as for the object of nihilistic denial: just as those who believe in false teachings constantly cling to the notion of non-self, they claim that all phenomena lack any characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
For this reason, by briefly explaining these six aspects of deviant attachment and slanderous extremes, the meaning of the Middle Way is revealed.
How, then, is the realization of all phenomena established?
As the sutra states: "Kāśyapa!
Illumination and ignorance are neither different nor distinct; to know them thus is called the Middle Way, the true and correct contemplation.
This extends even to the cessation of old age and death, which is non-dual and without distinction," and so forth.
There are three kinds of characteristics that explain and clarify the matter of realizing the Dharma;
these return to the three matters originally explained, as well as the fourth matter of causes and conditions, which includes both obstacles and their remedies.

Abiding in both the conditioned and the unconditioned, because they manifest that intrinsic nature and characteristics are unapprehendable, and because they manifest that superior matters are unapprehendable, as well as having cultivated these, they realize knowledge as it truly is.

Regarding the statement that "the characteristics of this neutral state are unattainable": it means that, as ordinary persons falsely conceptualize and cling to them, the essential characteristics of both clarity (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are unattainable.

Regarding the statement that "the superior reality therein is unattainable": it means that because all those falsely conceptualized and clung-to characteristics of ordinary persons—namely, cessation, arising, and aggregation—are not seen as having two distinct characteristics.

Regarding the one who has realized wisdom therein: because that wisdom, its basis, and the mental states associated with it are characterized by non-conceptualization; because their activity is unobstructed; and because they realize the selflessness of phenomena through internal wisdom.
How is the Bodhisattva’s realization of the Dharma explained?
It is because they turn their aspiration toward Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), and because it is also a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the statement, "If one does not cause all phenomena to be empty by means of emptiness," these seven phrases explain that for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, the Bodhisattva does not cause all phenomena to be empty by means of emptiness, nor do they abandon afflictions (*kleśa*); such is the meaning.
It is not by means of wishlessness that one causes all phenomena to be wishless, nor by means of signlessness that one causes all phenomena to be signless.
There is no further arising of karma or the flow of thoughts; all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are without intrinsic nature, and through the extinction of nirvāṇa, the worldly flow is ceased.
How is it that such practice establishes the state of not yet being free from the suffering of afflictions?
It is also by virtue of the meaning of the "single characteristic.

As it is said that all phenomena possess both existence and non-existence, so too are these seven phrases—concerning the dharmas of unextinguished enmities, obstructions, and so forth—expounded as the realization through observing them according to reality.

Regarding those who realize it as it truly is within this context: they return to those very phenomena, such as the hindrances, and—by means of the vision of the selflessness of phenomena through their essential nature and activity—are neither defiled nor [perceive them merely as] suffering.
In what way is this superior?
This is because it explains four kinds of characteristics:

demonstrating the excellence of vision; demonstrating the excellence of returning to that state through remoteness and separation; demonstrating the excellence of losing meditative concentration due to distraction; and demonstrating the excellence of mental agitation.
Regarding the superiority of this [view], the Sūtra states:
"Kāśyapa, it is not because there is no person that it is called 'empty'; rather, even the middle limit is empty. Thus, emptiness is taught not merely because one does not perceive a person."
Why is this so? Those who abide in the emptiness of sentient beings do not see the emptiness of phenomena; rather, they see that the very essence of phenomena is empty.

In the future, within nirvana, they will sever pride and skillfully contemplate the grasped object (*grāhya*) up to the point where the grasping subject (*grāhaka*) is understood through the wisdom of non-self, thereby becoming detached from the nature of conventional designations and being subsumed within emptiness.
Because they do not correctly observe the three times—past, future, and present—it is called "incorrect observation of the wisdom that knows *tathatā* and *jñeya*.

Due to their pride in falsely grasping phenomena through empty designations, they claim to rely on emptiness rather than the true emptiness of the selflessness of phenomena; because they do not extinguish their original grasping at the emptiness of sentient beings and their grasping at the arising of phenomena, they are said to have regressed from the characteristics [of realization].

Within this Dharma, the bodhisattva is not like that; for this reason, it is taught as superior, demonstrating the practice of the bodhisattva by revealing the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"You all should rely upon emptiness; otherwise, you will fall away from the Buddha-dharma."
Within this, there is this detachment, because it dwells superiorly in the selflessness of sentient beings.
The view of a self thus operates at the very lowest level among ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, that lowest level has two aspects:
First, not being exempt from suffering;
second, the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*). Because these are the two characteristics, it is said:
"Kāśyapa, it would be better to give rise to a view of a self as vast as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to overweening pride through the view of emptiness."
Why is this so? Kāśyapa!
All views are liberated through emptiness.
The passage, "If one gives rise to the view of emptiness, that cannot be cured," reveals this meaning.
It is better to give rise to a view of self as large as Mount Sumeru, for the view of self can be counteracted and brought to cessation.

One should understand that one does not give rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*) through the view of emptiness; rather, it is because one has not seen the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) that one gives rise to overweening pride.

By means of emptiness, I see that all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are empty; the nature of the grasping at false appearances is also empty, and even that which is empty of an unattainable essence is empty. Yet, one arbitrarily clings to the emptiness of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because one has arbitrarily established it in a state of inversion.
Because one clings to views in a distorted manner, the view of emptiness is established.
If the view of emptiness arises, it cannot be countered; therefore, it should be known that this [view] must not be maintained.
Because it cannot be sustained, one does not escape the various sufferings such as birth; for at all times, one is not free from the fever of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Thus, one is unable to practice with joy, being like an incurable patient.
Because the two kinds of grasping are extinguished, two kinds of characteristics are taught for those mentioned previously, just as a skilled physician administers medicine to a patient.
Even so, if one gives rise to the view of emptiness, I say that such a person is incurable.

This analogy illustrates the following: for example, just as a patient who does not properly attend to their recovery may aggravate various ailments, and due to the sequence of factors that either promote or inhibit the movement of the disease, they experience two kinds of painful sensations.

In this way, because the view of non-self in persons is not extinguished, it is equivalent to the view of self; furthermore, because the grasping at the selflessness of phenomena within the emptiness of persons is not abandoned, one naturally accords with the illness of the afflictions.
Because two kinds of extinction are apprehended sequentially, it is called "extinction."
The Bodhisattva is not like this.
Regarding the superior excellence of the cessation within this [state], it is as the sutra says: "For example, there is a person who fears empty space," and so forth.
It is like a person who, while in mid-air, engages in conceptual discrimination and false attachment, imagining objects and becoming terrified, and then speaks these words:
"Eliminate this emptiness, eliminate this emptiness," and so forth.

One who dwells thus within the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) does not abide in the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), because they give rise to fear due to the conceit of "I."

Regarding the sphere of infinite space, which is an ineffable matter, one erroneously clings to it as empty; having thus established this clinging, and because of that clinging and because of form and so forth, there arises the perception of form and so forth, whereby one seeks the cessation of those matters.
The Bodhisattva is not like this; because within this there is the superior matter of such mental distraction, it is said:
"Kāśyapa, it is as if a painter were to paint for himself the image of a terrifying yakṣa or ghost," and so forth.
Thus, those who have lost their practice and are distracted, because they abide in the view of personal selflessness (*pudgala-nairātmya*), conceptually discriminate that objects truly exist.
Due to such inversions of perception and so forth, they cause themselves to fall into error.
The Bodhisattva is not like that.
How does the Śāstra explain the cause?
It does so by means of two kinds of analogies:
The first is the analogy of the illusionist;
the second is the analogy of two pieces of wood rubbed together.

The initial analogy demonstrates that the wisdom realizing the selflessness of persons perceives only the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) as the grasper; when this [wisdom] is further examined by the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*), that wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena is termed both the grasper and the observation.

However, the wisdom of the non-self of persons and the wisdom of the non-self of phenomena serve as its causes; because those exist, this analogy is possible. If a magician and his illusory person serve as the causes, it is like the illusory person eating.

For a practitioner who acts in such a manner, the wisdom of the non-self of phenomena and the wisdom of the non-self of sentient beings are empty because they are free from the nature of conventional designations; they are quiescent because they are free from conceptual construction; they lack solidity because they are devoid of characteristics that can be grasped; and they are empty because they possess no substantial entity.
The second simile, "like eating," demonstrates the observation of non-substantiality.

For example, when two realities are realized, within that, the observation that realizes them as they truly are involves contemplating the stillness of both the grasper and the grasped; by not abandoning the causes of mindfulness and reflection, one eternally attains the arising of the definitive wisdom of internal knowledge.

In this context, that which is apprehended by insight (*vipaśyanā*) refers to the wisdom that contemplates the selflessness of sentient beings; that which apprehends refers to the wisdom that practices the selflessness of phenomena. These two are like the upper and lower pieces of wood [in a fire-drill], for they are mutually dependent.
Because tranquil reflection has tranquility as its cause, the internal realization gives rise to certain knowledge; this is called "realization of the truth.
These two similes of wood demonstrate that a cause can be obtained: just as fire is produced by rubbing two pieces of wood together, and once produced, it in turn consumes those two pieces of wood.

In this way, with the practice of the knowledge of the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena as its cause, the knowledge of the selflessness of phenomena arises; by means of internal wisdom as its object-condition, decisive knowledge is produced.
That nature of false conceptualization and clinging inherent in the practice of that knowledge is burned away through such contemplation of reality as it is.
How is it that "pervasive emptiness" is taught?
It is also because of the meaning of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*): by seeing things as they truly are within that very wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*).

The statement, "For example, when a lamp is lit, all darkness is naturally extinguished," is an explanatory simile for seeing things as they truly are therein; it means that ignorance and the like are devoid of the nature of conventional designations (*prajñaptisvabhāva*).
"Emptiness" is so called because of this non-apprehension.
"Inapprehensible quiescence" is so called because of non-awakening.
How, then, is that emptiness thus explained?
First, the extinction of karma leads to the extinction of afflictions, as this serves as the direct antidote.
When it says, "Kāśyapa, for example,
within a house— whether in a chamber, a room, or a dwelling— if there has been darkness for a thousand years or more," this is a metaphorical explanation for the various fetters and karmas.
Regarding the demonstration herein of "extinguishing until loss": the radiance of wisdom that arises immediately is able to extinguish all karmas and afflictions from beginningless time.
If one can thus swiftly extinguish all afflictions, for what reason does the Bodhisattva practice for such a long duration within the world?
The second analogy is presented to demonstrate the attainment of the supreme fruit.
When it says, "Kāśyapa!

It is as if seeds were sown in the air," up to "the various afflictions (*anuśaya*) and worldly dharmas can cause the Buddha-dharma to grow," this means that seeds can grow and flourish within a field of impure soil.

Through such analogies as these, it is shown that because this bodhisattva directs his mind toward nirvana, he does not abandon sentient beings; rather, for the sake of attaining the Buddha-dharma, he vows to take up the world. Having already dedicated and made vows regarding all roots of goodness, he practices the various deeds throughout the long night.
In this context, nirvāṇa is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and is likened to space; because bodhisattvas rely upon it, they do not cause the Buddha-dharmas to increase.

The world is like a field defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*), and the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of the bodhisattva is likewise like ground defiled by afflictions; by sustaining that ground, they are able to cause the Buddha-dharmas of the bodhisattva to grow.
Question:
How can one increase the unsurpassed Buddha-dharmas of a bodhisattva by relying on inferior conditioned phenomena?
To explain this through the analogy of the lotus, it is said: "Kāśyapa!..."
Just as lotuses grow from low-lying, muddy swamps, so it is with Bodhisattvas:
within the mud of saṃsāra and among sentient beings fixed in wrong determination, it is precisely there that Bodhisattvas give rise to the Buddha-dharma.
Question:
If this is so, then among the bodhisattvas, the śrāvakas lack these twelve kinds of superior qualities.
What are these twelve kinds?
That is to say: the excellence of cultivating the manifestation of various roots of goodness;
the excellence of cultivating the practice of wisdom;
and the excellence of attaining the liberation that is identical to the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising, which is subsumed within the fruit of liberation.
The supreme matters of extinguishing and subduing all Māras and adversaries;
the supreme matters of those beyond training (aśaikṣa);
and the supreme matters of the Arhats.
The supreme excellence of the assembly is taught in the sense of being "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat), based upon the four pairs of persons and the eight types of individuals.
The supreme excellence of the teachers is clarified by their teaching the Dharma for the attainment of Nirvana within this very life.

This clarifies the supreme excellence among sentient beings, extending from all sentient beings up to the nine abodes of sentient beings; likewise, it attains the supreme excellence of ultimate tranquility therein.

Regarding the supreme excellence of mastery over the mind and the supreme excellence of birth that is difficult to subdue, one should understand that various similes are taught to prevent difficulties.
To prevent the objection regarding initial victory, two similes of the great ocean and clarified butter are taught, because immeasurable sentient beings do not receive or utilize the similar Dharma.

Second, to prevent the objection, it is stated that the wisdom of a bodhisattva is twofold, as it serves as the antidote to the obstacles within both one's own body and those of immeasurable other sentient beings.
The third [section] is the protection against objections; it has two types. The analogy of the noble person should be understood as explained above in the section on liberation.
The analogy of the poor person refers to the various Śrāvakayāna practitioners and those with vows.
The station of a maidservant refers to not abandoning sentient beings.
The station of a king refers to the various vows of the Mahāyāna, which serve to protect against all enemies.
The initial analogy of the wheel-turning monarch refers to being a true son of the Tathāgata, thereby protecting the supreme state of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The second analogy of the wheel-turning monarch is for the sake of not severing the lineage of the Buddhas.
The protection of the superior state of the Arhat is for the sake of being worthy of offerings.
The third analogy of the wheel-turning monarch is taught for the sake of bestowing the cause of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience).

The protection of the superior and most excellent matters concerning the assembly is explained by means of the analogy of beryl (*vaiḍūrya*), because it first encompasses the attainment of the bodhicitta;
it is the protection of the speaker of the Dharma through these superior and most excellent matters.
The parable of the King of Medicine Trees is taught because it can remove the disease of afflictions for sentient beings.

Regarding the parable of the supreme excellence among those who protect and illuminate sentient beings: just as no one can abandon the lunar disc, so too [the Buddha] can produce the light of wisdom for all sentient beings.
The supreme matter of attaining protection and the most profound tranquility is likened to the new moon, because it gathers the causes of merit and wisdom to assist in the attainment of bodhi.
The supreme matter of attaining mastery over the mind through protection is likened to a lapis lazuli gem, because the bodhisattva thereby attains the fruit of sarvajñā.
Protecting against [regression] so that superior matters may arise again is like the treatment of a lapis lazuli gem;
as for the benefits such as mastery over the mind and the nourishment of the qualities of the śrāvakas, these depend upon the bodhisattva.
Thus, these various metaphors have been briefly explained to demonstrate the superior qualities of bodhisattvas among śrāvakas.
From this point forward, their various qualities will be explained in detail.
How many types of śrāvakas are there, and what are the superior features of the bodhisattva precepts within the context of the śrāvaka precepts?
There are four types of śrāvakas and furthermore thirteen characteristics; one should know that among the śrāvaka precepts, the bodhisattva precepts possess superior qualities.

Among these, the four types of śrāvakas are: the śrāvaka who follows by sound, the śrāvaka of self-conceit, the śrāvaka who makes the vow for enlightenment, and the śrāvaka of fixed extinction-nature.
Among these, those who are "śrāvakas by designation" are those transformed by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas for the sake of liberating sentient beings; they are called śrāvakas by designation.

Those who are "śrāvakas of self-conceit" are those who consider themselves pure solely because of their knowledge that sentient beings lack a self and their knowledge that there is no self-conceit regarding false dharmas; they are called śrāvakas of self-conceit.

Regarding those śrāvakas who form the aspiration for bodhi: if from the beginning their heart of compassion was slight, yet through proximity to the Tathāgata and through practice, they have cultivated within themselves the signs of merit through faith in the sublime and wondrous Buddha-dharma; although they have reached the ultimate state of abiding in untainted (anāsrava) precepts, the Buddhas exhort them by explaining various skillful means (*upāya*), whereby they are enabled to cultivate great bodhi.

Although they thus cultivate bodhi, because they are of dull faculties during their subsequent practice and because they delight in purity, they are not like those who possess the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) from the very first moment of generating the mind of awakening (*prathamacittotpāda*). For this reason, they are called "śrāvakas who aspire to bodhi."

Regarding the śrāvaka of fixed extinction: because from the very beginning his compassionate mind has been of a meager nature, because he is consistently averse to sentient beings and terrified by the suffering of the world, and because he dwells solely directed toward nirvāṇa, he is incapable of attaining the cultivation of great bodhi.

For example, there were two princes whose physical appearances were indistinguishable and who equally enjoyed all the pleasures of royalty; yet among them, one was thoroughly proficient in the royal laws, arts, and skills, while the second was not.

Because these two princes were superior among those skilled in the arts, they were not places for the enjoyment of pleasure; in the same way, it should be understood that Bodhisattvas dwelling in untainted precepts and Śrāvakas of the nature of cessation are likewise not such places.
Furthermore, there are superior matters within that body which should be known:

the locus for practicing all pure dharmas (*śukladharma*), the locus for the accumulation of wisdom, the locus of similarity, the locus of nature, the locus of family lineage, the locus of conduct, the locus of supernormal powers, the locus of cultivation, the locus of the field of merit, the locus of supreme excellence, the locus of cause and effect, and the locus of dependent arising—all these should be known.
For example, it is impossible for a seed sown in the air to grow; however, when sown in a fertile field free from weeds and impurities, it can indeed grow.
A lotus does not grow on high ground or dry land.
These and other such metaphors demonstrate the nature of the śrāvakas who are fixed in cessation and explain the superior matter of the bodhisattva’s sincere faith.

The śrāvaka fixed in cessation is like a ground covered in refuse; because they practice various mixed deeds within the defilement of the mud of various afflictions, they turn their backs on all sentient beings.

While the realm of nirvāṇa is like the earth remaining undisturbed even amidst a blazing fire, the Bodhisattva maintains a mind of equality and a mind of abiding toward the pure realm of sentient beings; conversely, he questions the mind directed toward nirvāṇa and the mind abiding in the purity of sentient beings. Because he does not abandon sentient beings who possess afflictions but seeks to deliver them, he takes up the defiled world and gathers in sentient beings. Although these states are mutually comparable as the locus for accumulating all pure dharmas, he manifests the performance of supreme deeds.
The śrāvakas possess only meager pure dharmas (śukla-dharma), benefiting themselves alone;
the dharmas of the bodhisattvas are immeasurable, benefiting and increasing all sentient beings as if they were their own children.

For example, just as a father nourishes his sons with fresh butter (*navanīta*), so too is the Bodhisattva: his own roots of goodness are immeasurable like fresh butter, and he nurtures and causes to grow newly initiated Bodhisattvas like his sons.
Space is the supreme manifestation of the accumulation of wisdom that reveals equality alone.
Because śrāvakas possess uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), they perceive only their own bodies as empty and quiescent.

Among all sentient beings, bodhisattvas—out of compassion—realize this same wisdom and dedicate it to all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, making vows to advance toward unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The parable of the chief consort and the maidservant demonstrates the distinction between the similar and the superior.

While the Śrāvaka contemplates and resolves upon liberation, the chief consort’s mother occupies a narrow and inferior position with a small mind; like a father who is impoverished, his mind increases [in such a way] that he does not become a son of the Buddha.

All bodhisattvas abandon the inferior nature of ordinary beings and regard them as their own servant-mothers; because they achieve this superior mindfulness through a mind like that of a consecrated great king, they are called "Sons of the Buddha."
The first analogy of the wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) demonstrates the excellence of the locus of the nature (*dhātu*).

Just as the son of a noble wheel-turning monarch may possess all powers, possess influence, and possess supreme majesty, yet because he lacks the physical marks of a wheel-turning monarch, he is incapable of becoming a wheel-turning monarch.

The śrāvakas are likewise: because they exert diligent effort, they achieve the various powers (*bala*); because they are skillful in the truths, they achieve influence; because they do not relinquish their resolve, they achieve supreme majesty; yet, because they lack the characteristics of buddha-nature, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not grant them protection or inclusion.
By means of the second analogy of the universal monarch (*cakravartin*), the Bodhisattva demonstrates the superior excellence of maintaining the Buddha-family.

Although the Śrāvakas have reached the ultimate limit, they are unable to maintain the Buddha-family in the future; however, the Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds (*prathamacittotpādika*) are capable of doing so.
The third analogy of the Wheel-Turning Sage King demonstrates the excellence of the place where practice is undertaken.

Although the Śrāvakas have attained ultimate perfection, the devas and sages do not honor and praise them as they do a newly practicing Bodhisattva; this is illustrated by the analogy of the Vaiḍūrya jewel, which demonstrates the ultimate excellence of the sovereign power of spiritual faculties.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, by means of wisdom and spiritual power (*ṛddhi*), the Bodhisattva surpasses all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The analogy of the medicinal trees on the Snowy Mountains illustrates the superior nature of their practice.
Although śrāvakas achieve the wisdom that can extinguish the disease of afflictions, it is the medicine of wisdom that extinguishes the afflictive diseases of sentient beings.
To counter-argue against the bodhisattva: it is because they exclusively and constantly practice for the benefit of others.
The parable of the constellations demonstrates the excellence of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).

Although they have reached the ultimate state of a *śrāvaka*, they cannot illuminate sentient beings with the light of wisdom; therefore, they do not function as a field of merit to deliver all humans and devas, unlike a Bodhisattva who, even while not yet extinguishing their afflictions (*kleśa*), serves as a field of merit for all humans and devas.
The analogy of the new moon illustrates the manifestation of excellence within excellence.

At all times, the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are eternally superior among the śrāvakas; yet, within that excellence, the bodhisattvas are further superior to them, because they arise from the bodhisattvas.
It should be understood that because Bodhisattvas possess two kinds of characteristics, they become increasingly superior.

In this way, they also transform and guide sentient beings and bring the Buddha-dharma to maturity; therefore, there is awakening and the attainment of the fruit, causing the beings they transform to attain liberation accordingly.
For example, it is like a craftsman creating a shadow-image that produces a sense of wondrous terror, yet does not consume the eater; this should be understood in the same way.
For example, it is like how all the gods and humans in the world well uphold lapis lazuli; this metaphor demonstrates the excellence of cause and effect.

Although śrāvakas single-mindedly cultivate and accumulate the superior causes of pure dharmas and further encounter and draw near to immeasurable spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), they are unable to attain the fruit of great bodhi.
To address the objection, it is said that "all bodhisattvas" are so called because they are able to attain the fruit of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
This is illustrated by the analogy of refining a *vaiḍūrya* gem, which demonstrates the superior matters arising from the basis.
All śrāvakas appear in the world because they rely upon bodhisattvas; it is not that bodhisattvas appear in the world by relying upon śrāvakas.
For the purpose of extinguishing evil and maintaining the meaning [of the Dharma], he addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"Kāśyapa, if in any land there are camels with black necks that look upward toward the light, then in that land there will be no such things as fear or dread."
"Therefore, Kāśyapa,
a bodhisattva should always protect and benefit sentient beings"— what gradual sequence is taught hereafter to demonstrate the superior matters of attaining those fruits and benefits?

As previously stated, the Buddha-dharma of a bodhisattva can grow within the mud of afflictions and defilements. If that is so, and it does not grow within that [afflicted] body itself, nor do the bodhisattvas cause it to assist within that body, how then can the Buddha-dharma of a bodhisattva grow within such a body?
For the sake of sentient beings, one cultivates various practices; this teaching is manifested for their sake.
If one causes those [beings] to increase, one also increases oneself.

As the Sūtra says, "A bodhisattva should always provide protection," and so forth; this demonstrates that reaching all worlds in the four directions, all bodhisattvas vow to bring benefit to sentient beings.

Regarding "the ultimate treatment of reality": all treatments for bodily ailments that lack a skilled physician, up to and including the treatments for afflictions provided by non-Buddhists, are called "non-real treatments" because they are merely conventional designations and because they are inverted.
In this context, it should be understood that the bodhisattva is likened to a skilled physician;

all sentient beings are like patients; the various illnesses are like greed and other afflictions; and the medicines are like the contemplations on impurity and so forth, because they possess three corresponding characteristics.

The great elements move and thereby give rise to various diseases; this occurs either because of the accumulation of various evils, or because of eating what should not be eaten, or because of neglecting the treatment of illnesses.

Thus, these three kinds of causes give rise to mental afflictions due to the characteristics of an evil mind; or because of the accumulation of various evils such as greed, and because of the habitual tendencies of greed and so forth throughout the long night.

Alternatively, it may be because one engages in what should not be practiced while seeing [it as permissible], or because one currently manifests the activity of various views and so forth, or because one abandons the practice of inverted matters.
Among these, it should be understood that for the first affliction-disease, the antidotes such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha*) are to be applied.
Impurity serves as the antidote for all forms of craving; loving-kindness serves as the antidote for ill-will; and the contemplation of the four causal conditions serves as the antidote for delusion.
Such teachings are expounded because illness exists, and thus their respective antidotes are taught.
The various types of emptiness and so forth are taught in reliance upon four kinds of sentient beings:
first, those who cling to views;
second, those who delight in and are attached to samāpatti.
Third, taking delight in various forms of birth;
fourth, conceiving the notion of liberation regarding that which is not liberation.

In this context, because sentient beings cling to various views, it is said: "All views can only be remedied by emptiness; yet if one gives rise to a view of emptiness," and so forth—this teaching should be understood accordingly.
Because they delight in and are attached to *samāpatti*, it is called "signless" (*animitta*), for there is no sign among all conceptualizations of existence and non-existence.

It manifests all existence and non-existence to demonstrate and cause attachment to *samādhi*. Because they rely on the joy of various births, it is called "wishless" (*apraṇihita*); because it extinguishes all [desires] of the desire, form, and formless realms, it is termed "wishless."
To regard that which is not a state of liberation as having the characteristic of liberation is not called one of the four perversions;
rather, the four perversions are taught for the sake of extinguishing all perversions, because they consist in the views of permanence and so forth.
One gives rise to the perception of liberation regarding that which is not liberation; this is because one abandons the habituation to perversion and relies upon the notion of a "possessor.
One should understand that the antidotes to the four perversions are explained both extensively and concisely.
There are further six types of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*):
for those who are attached to the body, the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are taught as their antidote;
for those whose afflictions (*kleśa*) are scattered, the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*) are taught as their antidote.
Because they are bound by mutual conceit (*māna*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are taught as their antidote;
because they have abandoned the cultivation of all virtues, the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) are taught as their antidote;
and because they do not penetrate the truths (*satya*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the path (*mārga*) are taught as their antidote.
Furthermore, because they serve as antidotes to the attachment to views concerning auspiciousness and inauspiciousness, the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are taught.

One should understand that failing to contemplate the body correctly leads to the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); if one does not discern the view of "mine" (*mamakāradṛṣṭi*), one turns away from the well-taught Dharma and lacks faith, and so forth.
To counteract those [afflictions], he spoke of the faculties and the powers. "Kāśyapa,
among all physicians and their disciples within Jambudvīpa, the physician-king Jīvaka is the foremost."
“Kāśyapa!

Suppose all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm were each like Jīvaka, the King of Physicians; even though such beings, resembling Jīvaka, might excel in demonstrating various treatises, medical formulas, extensive learning, and skillfulness, they would still possess the difficulty of being cured because they harbor views that are difficult to remove—such as grasping at views, teaching [others] to hold views, and harboring doubts and regrets—and because these views and the like act as obstacles to the concentration of mind achieved through skillful means.”
As the Venerable Chanda said: "Venerable sirs, I have had this thought:
'Form is impermanent,' and so on, up to:

'Furthermore, while I practice serenity (śamatha) that is empty and non-conceptual, within the cessation of craving, the fading away of desire, and Nirvana, my mind is not at peace, does not rejoice, does not abide, and does not find resolution; my intention turns back, giving rise to a mind of weariness and indolence."

However, when they say, "What then is mine?", at that time they recollect nirvāṇa with a mind of wisdom; yet because they have not extinguished the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), they think, "I shall cease to exist," and thus their minds regress from nirvāṇa and distress arises.
However, what is "I" or "mine"? One does not form such a thought;
these are merely conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
By what means, who, or for whom would they be non-existent?
However, because the worldly paths of practice at this time cannot cure it, it is called "incurable.
It is intended to encompass the mind that has not yet entered meditative concentration; by binding it with doubt and regret, it is able to dispel the causes of that doubt and regret.

Excluding those who provide instruction—namely, the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Bodhisattvas—who are free from all toxic afflictions and possess great power—it is said that [the others] possess only views, doubt, and regret;
they lack the power to awaken to it, their minds cannot fathom it, and they are unable to explain it, recite it, correctly teach it, or express it in words.
Having sought these practices for aiding the path, one seeks supramundane practice; seeking with a mind that still has remainder, there is subsequently further remainder.
Based on the selflessness of sentient beings, two types [of selflessness] should be known.

In accordance with the doctrine of selflessness (*anātman*), there are causes such as the wisdom that enters into a single object; one desires to have faith in fundamental wisdom and the wisdom of faith. Within this "mind-only," one should admonish and sever [delusions], for there is neither an object-condition nor a self to be realized.
Seeking within the conditioning of causes and conditions, one demonstrates the realization of the non-self of persons.

Because of the nature of deluded and discursive thoughts regarding the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*) and the corresponding stations of mindfulness and consciousness, the mind cannot be apprehended.
Furthermore, because one realizes the nature [of phenomena] through the accomplishment of formless characteristics and so forth, one manifests the realization of the selflessness of dharmas.
However, because this is an accomplishment of a nature that involves mental activity, there is still protection; for it does not involve incorrect grasping.
It says: "Kāśyapa!

Because the Buddhas do not perceive the entirety of the mind; because it is said that [the mind] is not self-arisen; because they do not perceive its manifestation as abiding in the essence of phenomena; and because all Buddhas speak of perceiving it throughout the three times."

Thus, it was previously stated that there is no nature of adventitious conceptualization; because those adventitious signs are shown as being explained through the signs of other-nature (parabhāva), and because they have a basis, it is merely said what their nature consists of.
Within this, the mind and mental factors are elucidated.

If one falls into the view that the mind is merely these signs (*nimitta*), how can it be explained that the world’s cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is like a magical illusion? This is what is being established.
The practitioner who dwells solely in this single mind is like a flowing river; practicing in this way with a mind of weary detachment, why would they not attain liberation?
The explanation for achieving this is like the wind.
Regarding "reaching far" herein, it should be understood that this is due to that very nature within all phenomena.
Since it is thus difficult to know, how can liberation be attained?
It is explained and established as being like a lamp flame.
Conditioned by the power of ignorance, there are volitional formations; because their exhaustion is manifested, they do not arise.
If the mind is defiled by the power of afflictions, it becomes stained;
otherwise, it accords with suchness.

Because those afflictions are impure, one does not perceive awakening or liberation; because one guards against this malady, it is manifested as being like space; because one guards against all maladies, it is like space, being without discrimination.

He manifests as being like lightning, perishing moment by moment, because he does not abide within greed and the other afflictions; he manifests the characteristic of impermanence, and he manifests the prevention of the affliction of divergent characteristics.
Although the pure mind perishes moment by moment, it manifests like a monkey; yet that [monkey] does not scatter because of a longing for various objects.
Therefore, greed and the other afflictions cannot be subdued, as they result in a state of distraction.
Why do all things not arise together simultaneously?
This is explained by the analogy of the painter.
Why do they not arise at all times?
Thus, by means of such [examples], the non-abiding nature of the creation of karma is established.
Why does one regress from present karma?

It arises either through the power of the fundamental or the manifest; this is explained as being like the affairs of a king. Since the power of cultivation regarding all karma is supreme, it perfumes the mind, thereby attaining predominance and being clearly expounded.
If it were like a king, why would he himself produce all these sufferings?
This is explained by establishing that he is like an enemy.
Why is he himself like an enemy?
The explanation establishes [the nature of] illness.

Because the household is manifested as a collection, there are four inversions manifested in the body and so forth; because they accord with such practices, the guarding against faults is of this kind.
For what reason does one take birth in a pleasant place?
It is because it is manifested as being like an enemy, because there are the three types of suffering, and because it is manifested that suffering arises even in that place.
Since such [states] are suffering, why not adopt the antidote to suffering?
This is shown because, like yakṣas and ghosts who seize a person's strength, they obstruct one’s attachment to the samādhi of bliss.
Furthermore, for what reason is it that, among the antidotes to non-delight, he does not manifest as one who acts like a thief by failing to guard against and failing to lead them away?
Because they are roots of goodness that assist the practice of the path.
If one dwells with the mental disposition that finds joy in performing meritorious deeds within suffering, by what affliction is this demonstrated?
It is like the occurrence of power and powerlessness, or of aversion and attachment.
Why? Because of delusion and madness.
Because of attachment to form and so forth, it is explained as being like a moth extinguishing a lamp.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa: "When one seeks the characteristics of this mind, they cannot be found; if they cannot be found, they cannot be seen.

Even so, the assembly of noble natures does not consist of bodily karma, nor of speech, nor of mind; within that nature there is no distinction of superior, middling, or inferior. When one seeks the characteristics of this mind, they cannot be found. What is the gradual sequence of this?

Having manifested the characteristics and activities of other-nature (*parabhāva*), because one seeks that other-nature according to its characteristics, one likewise seeks adventitious deluded thoughts; and when seeking the nature of accomplishment (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), that [other-nature] is manifested.
However, that nature of horizontal deluded conceptualization cannot be found when sought within the mind.

Therefore, its nature and characteristics are unattainable; because they are thus unattainable, the mind that is manifested as the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is then unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).

This shall be explained later; it demonstrates the manner of arising throughout the three periods of time, which is not like the mind at the moment of entering the meditative absorption of cessation that does not correspond to arising across the three periods.
Thus should the matter of that arising be understood, as it manifests the transcendence of the three periods of time.
It does not transcend the three periods of time, because once it has arisen, it gives rise to further moments of mind.
If it were to transcend the three periods of time, it could not be said to possess protection, as it would be grasping through arbitrary attachment.

The "manifestation" (nirmāṇa) mentioned alongside [the other two natures] exists and yet does not exist: it exists because it is the nature of false conceptualization and the perception of others; it is said to exist because it manifests the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
That which is "unborn" is non-existent because one observes the causes of the body.
"Nature" (prakṛti) refers to the cause that determines one's destiny in the hells and so forth.
"Those who have no destination" (agati) do not exist because [nature] acts as the cause for rebirth.
"Extinction" (niruddha) refers to that which has already ceased.
That which is "separated" does not exist, because it has ceased;
that which is "not separated" does not exist, because it has not yet ceased.
That which is "karmic activity" does not exist, because it refers to the aggregates (*skandhas*).
Regarding the statement "that is unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*): it is for the purpose of clarifying that [unconditioned state] that this "all of that is unconditioned" is taught.

Now, wishing to analyze and explain how this is the fundamental nature of all noble ones (*ārya*), it is because one attains that noble state through this mindfulness that the noble ones manifest by means of it.
However, that nature is manifested by both nirvana with remainder and nirvana without remainder, as well as by the nirvana of a bodhisattva.
Within this context, based on nirvana with remainder, it is said that there is neither the upholding of precepts nor the breaking of precepts.

Because one has well studied the precepts, there is no [further] practice; because extinction remains, it is not a state of having further practice; and because extinction remains, it is not the non-practice of the various afflictions.
That which is without mind and without mental factors is due to being free from defilement.
Regarding "action" (*karman*) herein, there is further the cause of affliction (*kleśa*) which consists of action.
Furthermore, regarding "no retribution for action," this is said in reliance upon *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder); it is for this reason that such a statement is made.
If there is neither suffering nor pleasure, that is the nature of the noble ones (*ārya*), as previously stated when it was said that "they have no karma.
The three sūtra passages explain the distinctions among those karmas.

The fourth phrase explains the distinctions among sentient beings; based on the *nirvāṇa* of the Bodhisattva, it states that this nature is equal like space, and so forth, up to "this nature is truly pure, for it has been ultimately pure from the very beginning."
That this nature is equal like space demonstrates its practice of equality, because it benefits both oneself and others; thus, this nature is without superiority.

That all dharmas have a single flavor demonstrates that he is no different from those pure bodhisattvas, and that he is no different in his excellence among all factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
That this nature is quiescent and detached, with body and mind in a state of tranquility, demonstrates that its essence is not distinct [from that state].
That this nature accords with and inclines toward nirvāṇa demonstrates that within the bodies of others, there is the excellence of that bodily karma.
"That nature is quiescent and far removed from all defilements" demonstrates that although it is identical to liberation, it possesses a superiority in the extinction of habitual tendencies.
"That nature is selfless and free from 'I' and 'mine'" demonstrates the eternal cessation of the pure world.

Regarding the statement that "this nature is without evil, whether empty or real, arising from equality," this demonstrates that within those practices, there is neither loss nor gain regarding the mundane world or nirvana, and no conceptual discrimination arises, because of the state of equality.
Because it is the ultimate reality, nirvāṇa is real;
because it is characterized by emptiness, one should know that the world is unreal.
This nature, which is the true ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), is demonstrated as being free from those [two] forms of denial and as not being shared with non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
That "this nature is inexhaustible and ultimately unarisen" demonstrates that although one attains *nirvāṇa* without remainder, one does not cease performing benefit for sentient beings.
Furthermore, that "this nature is ultimately unarisen" demonstrates that it is not born from afflictions or karma, but is born through the attainment of supreme sovereign power.
Regarding the statement that "this nature is eternally abiding and all *tathatā*s are eternal," this is shown to manifest both dwelling in the world and entering *nirvāṇa*.
Since those [manifestations] are not [the ultimate reality], one should know that this nature is taught to be blissful, pure, selfless, and so forth.
"The nature is truly pure and has been ultimately pure from the very beginning" is taught to demonstrate the purification of the *jñeyāvaraṇa* (obstructions to the knowable);
it reveals such purity in accordance with that which should be purified.
Therefore, one should understand the great significance of the distinctions between worldly and supramundane antidotes.
This should be understood as explained both through gradual succession and by means of skipping over stages.
“Kāśyapa! ‘A bodhisattva should benefit sentient beings in the four directions’” indicates that one benefits others by means of mundane and supramundane wisdom and so forth.
Regarding "reaching the four directions," what are these four directions?
They refer to traveling from one world to other worlds for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings.

By means of supernormal powers, one travels from one world to another just as one goes from one country to another; this is because one returns to those worlds to be born there, takes birth in various places therein, and causes others to become pure.
For the sake of purifying those sentient beings who are to be taught by those Bodhisattvas, they act as true and ultimate healers;
that is, Bodhisattvas treat afflictions by means of afflictions.

Because Bodhisattvas treat sentient beings who are like those suffering from great madness, they become unsurpassed supreme physicians; for they teach the three kinds of pure ethical conduct (*śīla*), which neither Jīvaka nor other great kings of physicians can cure, namely: the various views, as well as the removal of doubt and regret.
Alternatively, "greatly curing" (*mahā-vaidharya*) refers to being truly curative; thus it is called "greatly curing.

"Great" (*mahat*) means "true reality" (*tattva*). It is not by this [mere] meaning that one subsequently achieves true and ultimate cure; rather, it is accomplished by extinguishing the afflictions (*kleśa*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) through the practice of the supramundane path (*lokottara-mārga*).
Within this intermediate wisdom, there are two types:
first, the coarse;
second, the middling.
The coarse [level] serves as the antidote for the destruction of afflictions;
the intermediate [level] serves as the antidote for suppression.
Specifically, for those with excessive desire, the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) serves as the antidote.
Up to the point of extinguishing all inversions, there are four inversions that are thus extinguished.
The antidotes for coarse afflictions range from the four foundations of mindfulness to the eightfold noble path; the middling [antidotes] are those of suppression.
Among these, it should be understood that coarse afflictions transform into middling ones because they proceed as craving and so forth toward manifest objects. Regarding the practice therein:

by means of mundane wisdom, one guards against afflictions such as defilement within the characteristics of one's own objects; having subdued craving, one causes the nature of purity to function—this is the practice of the nature therein.

This is the distinction between the modes of conduct of the neutral: those who remain at home mostly engage in conduct characterized by greed, hatred, and delusion, while those who have left the home life mostly rely on various views.

Because they rely on those [views] and on the nature of improper mindfulness, they give rise to four kinds of perversions—both extensive and concise—through the discrimination of that nature of mindfulness; thus, in what is not a state of liberation, they produce the conceit of grasping at liberation.
Among these, greed and the like are purified by the contemplation of impurity as their antidote.
Hatred is countered by the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion.
Delusion is countered by the contemplation of causes and conditions.
Regarding various views, emptiness is the antidote.
Regarding conceptualization subsumed under improper mindfulness and conceptualization regarding the excellence of intrinsic nature, non-existence is the antidote.
Furthermore, for those who possess longing and aspiration, wishlessness is the antidote.
To produce liberation where there is no basis for liberation is not the antidote to error.
For example, if this place were permanent, yet afflictions exist therein,
what could prevent those coarse afflictions?

Based on their respective antidotes, one considers the objects of defilement—the matters of greed, hatred, and delusion—and the afflictions of greed and so forth that arise within present objects. "Accumulation" (*saṃskāra*) is the meaning of these formations;
because they must be extinguished, one cultivates the applications of mindfulness and other factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).

Because one practices the method of the foundations of mindfulness by binding [the mind] within right mindfulness, one practices so as to cause the unbound mind to attain binding of mindfulness; yet, one does not give rise to grasping in one's own mind through this mindfulness, saying, "I am practicing the foundations of mindfulness."
Having bound the mind within the various applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one practices right effort (*samyakpradhāna*) and takes up the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

Because of this taking up and abiding, one subdues the intermediate afflictions by means of internal knowledge and contemplation regarding the signs of male and female within the body and mind. By proceeding on the path through untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*), one employs supramundane dharmas as an antidote, thereby extinguishing lack of desire and other such states.
Based on the antidotes to desire and so forth, one does not allow the faculties and powers to function as views.

Regarding the ignorance that arises from the collection of causes and conditions and the ignorance regarding the selflessness of persons, these are suppressed by the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Thus, one becomes definitively established in the practice of what is not the right path and in the right path itself.
Thus, the knowledge of the objects that correctly prevent and subdue the coarse and medium afflictions associated with the characteristics of this realm is called mundane knowledge (*loka-jñāna*).
What is supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*)?

Thus, regarding the objects of defilement consisting of the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion that are to be subdued, as well as the knowledge of the remedial activities for all subtle underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), what are these?
Within those subduing remedies, there are three areas of skill: namely, the knowledge of the object (*ālambana-jñāna*), skillfulness (*kauśalya*), and causal conditions (*pratyaya*).

One gives rise to the wisdom of faith regarding the dharmas of non-self, non-sentient being, non-life, non-nourisher, and non-person; because one can trust that there is no self, one does not give rise to fear within the dharma of emptiness and non-discrimination.

Because one has faith in the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), a mind seeking [enlightenment] gives rise to diligence; all that exists is fully transcended, surpassing all afflictions (*kleśa*).
There are four types of remedial teachings:

because of not grasping due to a lack of wisdom, one contemplates the internal mind by applying the intellect to wisdom—namely, the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), defiled characteristics (*saṃkliṣṭalakṣaṇa*), and purified characteristics (*viśuddhalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding this lack of wisdom, one should understand that there are three kinds of perceptions (saṃjñā) which share the same meaning.
He seeks the mind in this way:
what is the mind?
That which is pleasurable, that which is subject to defilement, and that which is shameful belong to the past, the future, and the present.
