That which is past is called "exhausted"; that which is future has not yet arrived; and that which is present does not abide for even a single moment.
Among these, the minds conditioned by the past and future are entirely devoid of vitarka and vicāra; as for the present, it lacks vitarka in every moment.

Furthermore, one should know that various characteristics—such as those arising from greed and other factors through their own conditions, rather than being produced by the mind—are associated with the mind itself.

“Kāśyapa! This mind is not within, not without, and not in between. Because it is thus awakened, this mind cannot be found when sought; as previously stated, its nature is merely a provisional designation and is ultimately unattainable.
This mind is without color and without form; it has no abiding and no marks; it is indeterminate and unattached.

Thus, as previously stated, because one knows suchness through these six kinds of characteristics, all Buddhas have not seen it, do not see it, and shall not see it; and all noble ones do not perceive it through knowledge or vision.
One should know that the mind is associated with defilement because it manifests various characteristics.
Because it does not accord with reality and because it engages in various activities, the mind is like an illusion.

Arising from false conceptualization and discrimination, various karmic actions are produced; one undergoes various bodies and minds, receiving various forms of birth within the various realms of existence.
Because it does not conform to defilement, the mind is like flowing water.
As for its arising and ceasing without abiding, it returns to that very arising to flow in conformity with each successive thought-moment.
That the mind is like the wind traveling far and cannot be grasped means it is difficult to subdue amidst all thoughts.
Because it proceeds in accordance [with conditions], the mind is like the flame of a lamp.

When there is activity arising from various causes and conditions, it receives moisture with mastery; because it proceeds in accordance with defilement, and because it is able to act according to its course of action, this is the defilement of activity.
Where does the mind move like lightning?

It moves toward the places where one performs wholesome deeds; or, when a wholesome mind arises like lightning, the mind is like space, yet it appears as if empty because it is defiled by adventitious afflictions.
"The mind is like a monkey, for it is constantly greedy for various sensory objects.
The mind is like a painter, for it constantly gives rise to and performs all karmic activities. Kāśyapa!"

Regarding the statement, "The mind is not fixed and can pursue various afflictions": this means that even within a state of constant affliction, one may further engage in greed, hatred, and delusion, acting without abiding [in mindfulness].

The mind is like one traveling alone without a companion; it is not that it was originally possessed of defiled attachment and then became detached, nor that having become detached from desire, it possesses desire again.
Explanations such as these state that the mind is like a king because it attains mastery over all phenomena, and because it acts with the power of a sovereign within the realm of the Dharma.
The mind is like an enemy, for it can give rise to all suffering; it abandons its own happiness and is able to produce suffering.
The mind is like ashes, like a fishhook, like a dream, and like a blue fly; because it clings to what is non-self, it is able to produce suffering for itself.
However, because the perversions are like enemies that assist one's own suffering without ever being satisfied;
and because the mind is like a yakṣa ghost that robs others of their strength, causing one to abandon the cultivation of goodness as it seeks an opportunity.
The mind is like an enemy, for it practices unwholesome deeds and seeks out all manner of faults;
it constantly fluctuates between high and low status according to power and influence, and because it fails to understand the nature of love and hatred.
The mind is like a thief, for it leads one to negligence and can extinguish all roots of goodness, whether they have been performed or not.
The mind delights in various forms and so forth because it is attached to the objects of form and so forth.
Consequently, when one recollects the realm of the nectar that is eternally attainable, this recollection makes [the mind] difficult to settle.

One should know that the mind attains purity through three aspects: because of the non-attainment of the characteristic of attainment; because it is not a conditioned characteristic; because of the two kinds of signlessness; and because of the characteristic of the three natures.
“Kāśyapa! This mind cannot be found when sought.
Because it cannot be found, it cannot be cognized; this is called the nature of being unfindable when sought.
Because it cannot be obtained, it is not cognizable.
When the mind possesses such characteristics, and having contemplated this cause of mental purity, there arises a distinct mode of reflection.
When one seeks the purity of mind and cannot attain it, yet through such contemplation is able to attain it, this is called the characteristic of attaining what was unattained.
Thus practicing the cultivation of the selflessness of phenomena, and having so practiced, that which is realized by means of wisdom is the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The mind perceives through wisdom; subsequently, the characteristics of *tathatā* (suchness) are explained by means of nine aspects.
It should be understood that the nine unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) states are taught in contrast to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena.
That which transcends the three periods of time does not function as the three periods.
Furthermore, it is not like entering the meditative absorption of cessation, from which one can arise and subsequently give rise [to further states].

That it is neither existent nor non-existent is because its nature, designated by conventional names, cannot be differentiated or measured; for the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) can be known, as it is not characterized by those two [extremes].
That which is non-arising is so because it lacks the characteristic of arising.
That which is without intrinsic nature is so because it transcends the causal characteristics of the nature of arising.
That which is without origination is so because it has transcended all forms of arising within the future.
That which is without cessation has transcended death within the limits of分段 (paryāya-maraṇa).
That which has nothing to be abandoned has transcended the abandonment of moment-to-moment thoughts.
That which has nothing to be abandoned is neither coming nor going.
"Non-retrogression and non-arising" refers to having transcended the various paths of transmigration.
"The absence of karmic activity therein" refers to having transcended karma and afflictions.
That which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the noble lineage (*āryagotra*).
This neutral characteristic should be understood as the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*), for by seeing it, the various noble matters (*ārya-vastu*) are revealed.
Furthermore, within that present dharma, it transcends the five things, being the nature of the noble ones (*āryatva*).
There are no observers of precepts, because they have transcended the act of performing them.
There are no violators of precepts, because they have transcended non-action.
There are no practitioners, because they have transcended the act of practicing.
It is not that there is no practice, because one has transgressed by performing non-practice;
nor is it that there is no practice, because one has transgressed by failing to perform practice, and because there is the transgression of existing in the future.
This state of being without mind and without mental factors transcends all further arising, because it does not initiate volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
It is without initiation because it transcends those formations.
Regarding "no karmic retribution," this is because they have transcended birth in a [specific] family.
Regarding "they have neither suffering nor pleasure," this is because they have transcended the dependence on power or lack of power.

Within this, there is no karma and no activity that gives rise to karma; yet, within that nature, there is no action performed by body, nor by speech, nor by mind, because it is based on the movement and fluctuation of all that is conditioned by suffering and pleasure.
"Non-action" means transcending all precepts of training.
"The absence of the activity that gives rise to karma" means transcending all vows.
Furthermore, within that nature, there is no action of the body and so forth, because it transcends the receiving of retribution.
Within that nature, there is also no distinction of superior or inferior, because it transcends those various bodies upon which it depends.
Nevertheless, one should understand that it possesses a nature characterized by four periods and nine types of distinctions.

The times of impurity, purity, realization, and exhaustion—this nature is equal to space. During the time of impurity and so forth, it reaches all marks; like space, like the pervasive void, such is the *tathatā* within all forms and all marks.
"Manifestation" refers to seeing meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*) at the time of purity; this is the time of impurity.
"Single characteristic" is the nature of non-conceptuality, because all phenomena are of one flavor (*sama-rasa*).
This nature is quiescent and detached from the body.
When the mind is quiescent and pure, it is because of the single flavor and the quiescence of both body and mind.
It should be understood that there are two types of purity at this time.
This characteristic is quiescent because it accords with and leads toward *nirvāṇa*.

This nature is pure and far removed from all defilements of affliction because it is eternally realized; therefore, through this accordance and purity, when one accords with and proceeds toward the point of final attainment, that is called the "time of realization."
The first characteristic—that which is not separated from the nature of "self" and "what belongs to self"—is the second characteristic within the context of transcending the realization of the body.
That this nature is without evil, whether illusory or real, and arises from equanimity, is because it transcends those fundamental evil views; thus, it corresponds to the third characteristic.
This nature, which is the true reality and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), refers to the time of eternal cessation.
Those who abide within that cessation are eternal and achieve all forms of bliss, because they have transcended the three kinds of transformation.
Within this, there are three kinds of transformative processes:
first, the transformation of birth and death and so forth;
second, the transformation of the locus of inversion.
Third is the transformation of the regression from purity.

As for "this nature is inexhaustible and ultimately non-arising," it refers to the transcendence of transformations such as birth and death; this is called the first sign within the stage of the accomplishment of exhaustion.

Regarding this nature that is eternally blissful, pure, and non-self: because it transcends the state of perversion through transformation, it returns to that subsequent exhaustion, which is the second characteristic within the middle stage.

Regarding this nature that is truly pure and ultimately pure from the very beginning: because it transcends the state of regressive purity through transformation, it returns to that exhaustion, occurring at the time within the middle stage, which is the third characteristic.
Therefore, up to the point of manifesting the practice of mundane and supramundane paths to benefit others, it is said: "Kāśyapa!
You should observe within yourself; do not flee outward."
"Up to this point, Kāśyapa!
A bhikṣu practicing the Path should seek liberation from whatever binds his mind.
"Kāśyapa! [he continued].
Regarding the phrase "you should observe within yourself," what is its gradual sequence?

Just as those noble ones (ārya) who have purified themselves through the manifestation of that very nature have already demonstrated suchness (tathatā), so now, following that suchness, the one born as a noble one provides the answer by explaining it clearly.
Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra Śāstra, Volume Three;
Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra Śāstra, Volume Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of North India during the Later Wei Dynasty.
“Kāśyapa! There will be bhikṣus in the future who are like dogs chasing clods of earth. In this context, those who are like dogs are the non-Buddhists;

the five kinds of sensory objects, such as form and so forth, are the clods of earth; and “throwing” them is like being terrified by forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles—manifesting fear toward these various sensory objects.
Because he fears objects and does not realize the cause of that fear, he manifests four kinds of signs and pursues only objects.
One who dwells in a secluded place does so because they desire to transform and attain superior objects, thereby taking up a secluded abode.
He dwells alone without equal, having eliminated those defilements and abiding forever in non-duality; though his body is detached from the five desires, his mind does not abandon them.
At times, this person may think of pleasant sounds, fragrances, tastes, or textures; because he does not observe within and lacks awareness, a subtle attachment of greed arises.
Recalling various sensory objects, they remain unaware because of their forbearance.
How then can they become free from form, sound, scent, taste, and touch?

Because they do not know and do not perceive, when they later enter cities, villages, royal capitals, and the like among the masses of people, they are once again bound by the five desires of beautiful forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and touches; therefore, they fall back once more.

If one dies in a secluded place, because they have maintained the mundane precepts, they will be reborn in the heavenly realms, yet they will be bound by the attachment to the five sensual pleasures of those higher heavens.
Furthermore, when their life there ends, they will not escape the four miserable destinies.
What are these four?
They are the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras.

One should know that falling from birth among the devas is entirely due to conduct based on craving, which constitutes the "black faction"; it is due to conduct based on views that one should know as the "white faction."
Because one perceives the selflessness of persons, it should be understood that the two types of black and white factions and so forth are established as their respective antidotes.
Having thus cultivated these practices, one should cause the distracted mind to be gathered, and once gathered, cause it to attain liberation.

In this context, the sūtra passages employ metaphors because liberation is attained through a mind that does not enter meditative absorption; thus, various skillful means of śamatha are taught, including the śamatha of adopting and abandoning the afflictions. To remedy the mind characterized by such conflicting states, the metaphors of the throat and the bound person are explicitly explained.

Within the concentration of a single mind, it explains the means for liberation and manifests the characteristics of seeing and cultivation; because it teaches the means to extinguish afflictions within them, those [afflictions] obstruct the body-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the delight in *samādhi*, as is known through analogies such as the throat and the binding.
Because one employs supramundane wisdom when realizing the Truths, it should be understood that the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is like a disease in the throat.
Since such practices prevent the existence of dharmas such as "prevention" and so forth, two metaphors for emptiness are taught regarding the impure mind:
first, the recitation of worldly non-Buddhist scriptures and various treatises; [and second, the practice of asceticism].
Second, because of the practice of accumulating many fine robes and bowls based on one's occupation and physical body;
these two factors can cause one to obtain two kinds of bonds, respectively:
first, the bond of views (dṛṣṭi-bandhana).
Second, the fetters of gain, honor, fame, and so forth.
These two types of fetters act as obstacles to prevent unarisen wholesome dharmas from arising; one should therefore attain two kinds of dharmas:
first, the fellowship of the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa).
Second, by associating with various donors, one causes already arisen wholesome dharmas to be extinguished and defiled, thereby incurring two kinds of impurities:
first, the impurity of tolerating various afflictions; [and second, the impurity of being corrupted by them].
Second, by coveting various donors, acquaintances, and so forth, one forever severs and uproots the dharmas that are the roots of goodness;
this causes others to assist in obtaining two kinds of rain and hail that destroy the Dharma:
first, slandering the True Dharma.
Second, those who break the precepts yet accept the offerings of the faithful cannot be cured in this present life; consequently, they incur two kinds of sores:
first, they seek out the faults of others.
Second, one conceals one's own transgressions.
Because of these evil deeds that bring suffering in the present life, one incurs two kinds of burning conditions:
first, having a defiled body and mind while wearing the saṃghāṭī robe;...
Second, receiving the prostrations, offerings, and so forth from others who possess the merit of upholding the precepts.
Regarding the future, because one cannot give rise to [wholesome states] whether they are obtained or not, it causes one to incur two kinds of incurable diseases:
first, harboring overweening pride while suppressing one's own mind; [the second being...]
Second, they destroy others' resolve for the Mahāyāna by slandering bodhisattvas;
therefore, it should be understood that there is a further gradual sequence based on the śrāvaka precepts in the future.
"Kāśyapa!..."

Regarding the phrase "one should observe within oneself," and so on up to "who among these is wise," this explains the analogies for superior ethical conduct (*adhiśīla*) and extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), because they serve to subdue greed, affliction, and the like.
Because they give rise to a sense of revulsion and remorse, they clarify the training in higher mind (*adhicitta*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*).

As for the analogies of the throat and the bound person, because of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), they clarify the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) and ethical discipline.
If it is asked why the practice of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*) is taught here when the sūtras describe it as the ethical discipline for subduing afflictions such as greed,
the answer is:
because it is capable of initiating the conduct that leads to such afflictions.

Transgressions are mostly initiated by the characteristics of greed, hatred, and delusion; therefore, it is said that subduing greed, affliction, and so forth constitutes the practice of superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*). Question:
How do greed, affliction, and so forth cause transgressions to be initiated?
Answer: Because there are two kinds of characteristics.
For example, they are unable to perform repentance; [the other is]...
Just as that confession does not constitute a true confession,
so too there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, because they do not understand the cause of the afflictions, feel fear toward sense objects such as forms.
Dwelling in a secluded and empty place, because unwholesome thoughts arise within one's own mind, one also gives rise to the realms of greed, affliction, and pride.

Or, if one directs mindfulness toward other objects and perceives greed and so forth, they will pursue them like a dog chasing a clod of earth; because it is struck by the clod, the dog pursues only the clod.
In this way, because greed and the like have not been eliminated, if one forms present mindfulness through such matters as intimacy with villages and the like, this is called "not yet eliminated.
Because it accords with the meaning [of elimination], it is called "eliminated" and "completely eliminated."

Why is it that among the "black faction" (kṛṣṇapakṣa), greed (*lobha*) is said to be subdued while affliction (*vyāpāda*) is not, whereas among the "white faction" (śuklapakṣa), affliction is said to be subdued while greed is not?
The answer is:
because both belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is shown that there is partial subduing and partial non-subduing.

He manifests that some are disciplined while others are undisciplined; if one should pass away while in a secluded place, because they are thus undisciplined, even those who abide in the precepts will be ruined, for they have failed to achieve the higher training in ethical conduct (*adhiśīla*).
How much more so for those who do not abide in the precepts, like a horse that has left the path or gone astray.

In this way, when a practitioner practices higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*), even a single erroneous thought is called "distraction," for it can sever the life-faculty (*jīvita-indriya*) just as a disease of the throat can end one's life.

Likewise, when relying on the practice of non-self (*anātman*) to cultivate higher wisdom (*adhijñāna*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) can sever the life-faculty of the Dharma, just as a person seeks liberation from whatever place they are bound.
Thus, by means of superior wisdom regarding the practice of selflessness according to the Dharma, one causes the mind to be reckoned as liberated from deluded thoughts according to its nature.

Within these three types of cultivation of precepts, there are eight kinds of factors that contravene the precepts and eight kinds of factors that accord with impure states of mind: namely, reciting worldly and non-Buddhist scriptures and treatises, and having many fine robes and alms bowls, which are of no use [to liberation].
Just as space is adventitiously defiled, this adventitious defilement is the cause of bondage; therefore, two kinds of bondage are explained in succession:
first, the bondage of views;
second, the bondage of fame and gain.
This sequence is taught because it serves as the cause for bondage;
due to the fetter of views, one hates and slanders the assembly of the noble ones,
and for the sake of gain and fame, one associates with laypeople.
Because they are the causes of defilement and obstruction, two kinds of defilements are explained in succession:
first, hating, resenting, and slandering the noble assembly while tolerating various afflictions;
second, due to associating with laypeople, coveting donors, acquaintances, and the like.
Because these defilements are caused by rain and hail, rain and hail are discussed next.
Because they tolerate various afflictions, they slander the True Dharma.
Out of greed for donors and due to the conditions of associating with those who break the precepts, it is said that those who break the precepts receive the offerings of the faithful.

Because of the causes of rain and hail, there subsequently arise boils and sores; this is due to slandering the True Dharma and accepting the faithful offerings of others while violating the precepts, as well as concealing one's own transgressions.

Because the cause is the burning and boiling of ulcers and sores, the method of burning is explained next: seeking out the faults of others while wearing the saṃghāṭī robe with a defiled body and mind, one uses it to conceal one's own transgressions and thereby receives the prostrations, offerings, and respect of others who possess the merit of observing the precepts.

Because they are the cause for burning away the roots of merit, the incurable diseases are explained next. Thus it is said that those with defiled bodies and minds who wear the *kāṣāya* robe harbor overweening pride (*adhimāna*) while accumulating a mere semblance of discipline; because they accept the prostrations, offerings, and so forth performed by others who possess the merit of upholding the precepts, they destroy the resolve of others who abide in the Mahāyāna mind.
Regarding this, it is said that the "white faction" (śuklapakṣa) should be understood.
Among these two types of persons, the first is to be known as one who practices through vision (dṛṣṭicarita), and the second is to be known as one who practices through craving (tṛṣṇācarita).
By what sequence are the four kinds of śramaṇas demonstrated?

Just as with those afflictions that violate the precepts—whether through association or avoidance—and having encountered either human afflictions or human virtues, these become obstacles within one's mindfulness.

Alternatively, regarding those who are not obstacles, it is shown that among these people there are three types of afflictions; one should know that this is taught in reliance upon these three types of persons.
As for those who are śramaṇas in appearance and dress but whose minds and conduct are both ruined, this is taught according to the meaning of relying on [afflictions] due to their delighting in evil.

Deceptive śramaṇas and those who are śramaṇas in name only practice [the path] while their minds are corrupted; they rely on two kinds of delighting desire: great delighting desire and the desire for existence.
Among these, the evil of delighting desire is when one claims to be a śramaṇa while not being a śramaṇa.
Regarding those who fear greatness: if one possesses various virtues, yet their own mind overestimates those virtues, they should constantly maintain this thought.
Regarding those who possess joy and desire: if one possesses virtues, they should give rise to a mind that regards those virtues as equal to their own.
Regarding the first, there are two kinds of destruction of conduct:
first, that with remainder;
second, that without remainder.
Regarding "there being others":
it should be understood that this is spoken in reference to the four types of śramaṇas.
It refers to those who, based on their reception of the precepts, [possess] outflow-tainted states up to the performance of impure mental karma.
Regarding these three types of unwholesome lack of discipline, they are demonstrated respectively as follows:
based on begging for alms, "impure livelihood" is taught;
based on enjoyment, "miserliness," "enjoyment of possessions," and "hoarding and storing up" are taught.
Based on the practice of activities, "impure livelihood" is spoken of;
based on enjoyment, "miserliness," "enjoyment," and "storing up provisions for the night" and so forth are spoken of;
and based on the practice of activities, "laziness" is spoken of.
"Without remainder" refers to [the destruction of] the precepts due to breaking them, and because of teaching others to commit root offenses.
"Corrupting the mind" refers to [the presence of] unwholesome dharmas and the concealment thereof.
Secondly, regarding the accomplishment of practice, one should understand that it consists of livelihood based on conduct, the observance of precepts, and the cultivation of the path.
Among these, the accomplishment of practice is so called because it relies upon conduct.
One who has accomplished the objective sphere does so by virtue of life-force.
One who has accomplished dignified conduct does so by means of the four modes of action with a defiled mind.
One who relies upon the precepts is characterized by few desires because they consume coarse and unpalatable food.

Regarding the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*): they are established by virtue of [noble] enjoyment; by virtue of not associating with various monastics or laypeople; and by virtue of cultivating the path.
They consist of speaking little and talking little, and delighting in tranquility.
One should understand that although they practice such dharmas as consolation and so forth according to the treatises,
these are all for the purpose of deception and not for the sake of a virtuous and pure mind, because their minds are corrupted.
One should know that because they rely on the practice of [erroneous] conduct, they are deceptive.
Those who constantly possess the view of a self do not eliminate the practice of the view of a self by relying on the selflessness of persons.
They give rise to fear and dread toward the teaching of emptiness, as if facing a deep pit.
Relying on the non-self of phenomena, they do not discern emptiness, and they conceive thoughts of enmity toward those who teach it.
One who has accomplished the practice of a third person abides in accordance with mindfulness; it should be understood that this relies upon and accords with the various dharmas.
In this context, "abiding" refers to maintaining the precepts, and "mindfulness" refers to extensive learning; because one is mindful of those, one attains accord with all matters.
As for the basis: one sits in a secluded place; because of sitting in seclusion, one accords with all meritorious qualities.
To accord with all dharmas means to have few desires, to be easily contented, and so forth.
One should understand that this contradicts the mind regarding one's own kin.
In this context, the statement that "various thoughts are not extinguished" indicates the manifestation of weary detachment from desire.
Because it serves as their antidote, it extinguishes the blazing afflictions and so forth, for the sake of attaining the three types of perfect enlightenment (*sambodhi*).
The cessation of the three [poisons] is *bodhi*, because it is the fruit of the practice of the Path.
The fourth person accomplishes both; this should be understood through the power of nine kinds of accomplishment:
first, the power of constant practice;...
2. the power of extensive learning;
3. the power of aspiration;
4. the power of tranquil reflection;
5. The power of right view;
6. The power of realization;
7. The power of cessation.
8. The power of cultivation;
9. The power of correct realization.
Regarding "not seeking body or life," it should be understood that because one does not cherish body or life, this is called the power of constant practice.
"One who delights in hearing the Dharma of emptiness and so forth and whose mind is joyful" clarifies the second power of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).

Such a person does not even take pleasure in views of emptiness and the like, nor do they take pleasure in practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) for the sake of nirvāṇa, let alone seeking after the triple world (*tridhātu*).
One does not seek after various views, for those phenomena should also be extinguished.
Because one intends to attain nirvāṇa through that fruit and that path, the third desire-potency is taught.
Constantly relying on the Dharma and not relying on words or phrases, all afflictions seek internal liberation rather than fleeing outward.
Because one relies upon the Dharma, one seeks meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), reflection (*cintā*), mental states, and worldly wisdom (*laukika-jñāna*).

The power of the fourth [stage], the contemplation of tranquility (*śānta-manasikāra*), consists in constantly seeking liberation from all afflictions (*kleśa*) without looking outward; it perceives that the original nature of all phenomena is stainless and ultimately pure, such that one relies upon oneself and not upon others, because one's nature is undefiled.
The learner (śaikṣa) knows and sees the supramundane dharmas within themselves.
By the power of the fifth right view, one does not even perceive the Dharma-body, let alone the form-body, because the Three Jewels are not perceived.
The true Triple Gem is also distinguished by means of supramundane wisdom; this is the sixth power of realization.

Because one does not perceive any phenomena through the detachment from the affliction of emptiness, how much less could one be greedily attached to sounds or verbal expressions? This is because that which ought to be eliminated has been extinguished.
The seventh power of cessation refers to that which is not to be cultivated because it has already been cultivated.
The eighth power of cultivation consists in neither arising in saṃsāra nor clinging to nirvāṇa; knowing that all phenomena are originally quiescent, one perceives no bondage and seeks no liberation.
Therefore, one neither abandons the world nor realizes nirvāṇa, because the causes of the world have been extinguished and nirvāṇa has been attained.
Thus, one neither arises in the world nor seeks nirvāṇa; one neither longs for death nor for life, and seeks neither liberation nor bondage, for these have already been extinguished.
Furthermore, because there remain other factors, they neither proceed nor cease.

One should know that the various dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), which are subsumed under the knowledge of the extinction of outflows (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), constitute what is called the ninth power of authentic realization.

All those three kinds of śramaṇas who assume the name "śramaṇa" do so without its true meaning and with a semblance that is inconsistent with reality; because they are struck down by their own names, the analogy of poverty is taught.
Why is it called "that which is felled by name"?

Because their outward appearance and robes differ from those of true śramaṇas, they falsely accept the offerings and sustenance of faithful donors; from this point on, they are no longer śramaṇas who practice in accordance with reality. Furthermore, because they recognize those who practice in accordance with reality and give rise to pride toward them, and because they maintain the precepts while possessing a perverted understanding that makes their practice appear as if it were the genuine observance of the precepts.
Regarding the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, two similes are taught based on the pride that arises from them.
For example, there is a person who is swept away by a great flood and dies of thirst;
this simile demonstrates how the pride of "I" arises because one possesses the wisdom of hearing.
The analogy of the physician is used because, due to possessing the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), he delights in and clings to *samāpatti*.
Ordinary persons who have abandoned desire delight in and cling to gain and honor.
Regarding those learners who give rise to regret and cultivate *samāpatti*, it is because they practice wisdom in a distorted manner.
To demonstrate that even while practicing the correct path one may give rise to *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am"), three further similes are taught.
The first is called the Parable of the Sick Man;
the second is the Parable of the Jewel;
and the third is the Parable of the Dead Man. Because they give rise to pride based on their observance of the precepts, these demonstrate the four types of bhikṣus who violate the precepts.
Regarding the analogies such as "properly upholding the precepts" and so forth: among these, the first refers to the provisional reception of the precepts;
the second describes the failure to uphold the Vinaya clearly due to negligence;
and the third, because its practice resembles that [negligence], refers to the "corrupted precepts" which obstruct and destroy [the path] due to the breaking of the precepts.
The fourth is said to be the possession of the twelve dhūta qualities; this is the nominal observance of the precepts.
Among these, the first refers to seeing the afflictions that destroy the precepts as obstacles to their remedy; thus, it should be understood as "the destruction of the precepts."

Because they have broken the precepts, they cannot maintain even one among them; they give rise to fear regarding nirvāṇa and are unable to extinguish the obstacle of broken precepts, and thus they practice the remedies.

The second [point] is that because of the conceit of "I" (asmimāna), one gives rise to the appearance of having attained liberation; to counteract this, the true merits of upholding the precepts are taught.

Now, regarding what is manifested by the evil of breaking the precepts and what is manifested by the practice of the path of cultivation, herein, for the sake of those who first uphold the precepts, it is said that these are internal bases (ādhyātmikāyatana) and not external bases.

The second [point] explains that defiled karma consists of both action (*kriyā*) and non-action (*akriyā*), whereas wholesome non-action is not produced by the body and so forth; likewise, defiled karma also possesses both action and non-action. This is because it can produce wholesome states that are neither active nor inactive, depending on whether they are defiled or undefiled. Depending on whether one partakes of alms-food in a defiled or undefiled manner, there is neither activity nor non-activity. Because of this partaking—whether defiled or undefiled—there is the nirvāṇa without remainder, which is without name or form. It is without perception and without non-perception, for within the practice of signlessness (*animitta*), all perceptions have been detached from discursive thought.

Furthermore, mindfulness is characterized by the absence of conceptualization, where neither cessation nor non-cessation occurs; for while there is no remainder of conditioned formations within *nirvāṇa* with remainder, there is no remainder of afflictions.
It is without grasping or abandoning, because it constantly operates in detachment from joy and sorrow, and because equanimity and mindfulness arise together.

There is nothing to be grasped and nothing to be abandoned; one returns to that original state, because neither sorrow nor joy is grasped, and the notions of grasping and abandoning arise simultaneously.
There are no sentient beings and no names for sentient beings, even up to the point where there is no mind.
The absence of mind is called the "explanatory metaphor based on [the cessation].

Since the capacity for designation has ceased, as well as that which is designated and that which designates, there is neither the mundane nor the non-mundane, because it is based upon the world-receptacle where the practices of practitioners—both mixed and unmixed—are carried out.
To speak of neither having a basis nor not having a basis refers to relying on both the defiled and the non-defiled, as well as the objects of the six consciousnesses which are like village fields.
To speak of not exalting oneself through precepts and not slandering the precepts of others refers to relying on [the practice of] associating with households.

Furthermore, one does not recollect or conceptually discriminate that precept; one does not discriminate, "I am one who upholds the precepts," nor "I possess such upholding of precepts," because one does not discriminate that intrinsic nature.
The untainted (*anāsrava*) is also that which can be extinguished in common with the world, yet because it is manifested immediately, it is called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*).

However, if those [untainted states] are neither the fruit of the three realms nor the sought-after cause of the three realms—these two phrases are shown to illustrate this—and this is what is meant by "gradual succession."
Because there are dharmas that are concordant or discordant with the precepts, the distinction between well-trained and poorly trained śramaṇas is taught.
Who is the poorly trained śramaṇa?
In this regard, three types should be known.
First, those who resemble śramaṇas in outward appearance and dress, yet do not cherish the śramaṇa precepts;
they may share the same appearance and dress as others, but their physical life, livelihood, and enjoyments are not similar to their vows for life, their precepts, their views, or their minds.
In this context, because of the similarity in physical form and attire, it is called "similarity in form and attire.
Regarding the point of attire here, it is called "sameness of attire" because of [wearing] the *saṃghāṭī* and other such robes.
Regarding "form and appearance": because they have shaved their hair and beards and carry alms bowls, they are said to be identical in form.
Because of their impure physical actions and so forth, they are said to be dissimilar in conduct.
Because of impure livelihood, their lives are dissimilar.
Because of stinginess, they are dissimilar in their enjoyment of resources.
Because of laziness, they are dissimilar in their practice.
Because they have broken the precepts, they do not resemble those who uphold them;
because of their unwholesome dharmas, they do not resemble those with right view;
and because their faculties are undisciplined, unsubdued, and unrestrained, they do not resemble those whose minds are composed.
Regarding the second type, the śramaṇa who deceives through outward demeanor:

one should understand that while his requisites for alms and his application of diligence are appropriate, his higher mind (*adhicitta*) and higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) do not correspond to those practices, because he accomplishes them through the employment of artifice and the like.
They are equal in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*), because they are serene and composed in mind, and so forth, up to not delighting in distraction.
They are equal in the practice of higher mind (*adhicitta*), because they speak little and converse sparingly.
Their superior intellectual conduct is the same, yet their mental engagement differs because they are characterized by deceit and fraud.
The third type, known as the "renowned śramaṇa," should be understood as one who seeks only fame and reputation.

The factors of śamatha are identical, the factors of vipaśyanā are identical, the cultivation of those two parts is identical, and even their auxiliary practices are identical; yet the nature of the mind is not identical.

In this regard, by virtue of morality (*śīla*) and because it constitutes the factor of morality, it is identical to the factor of *śamatha*, for morality is the cause of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
By virtue of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), it is identical to the factor of *vipaśyanā*, for hearing enables one to acquire untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Because they dwell in secluded forest hermitages (*araṇya*), those two types of cultivation are similar and identical, for they both rely on dwelling in seclusion as the cause of their practice.
Their auxiliary practices, such as having few desires and so forth, are likewise identical, because those qualities like few desires serve as aids to the practice of training.
Because they associate with others, it should be understood that their minds do not correspond [to the Dharma].
Who is a well-trained śramaṇa?
It should be understood that there are four types.
Because of practice, because of the mind, because of realization, and because of reaching the ultimate limit.
This is because, by not begrudging one's body or life, one attains the practice of weariness and remorse within the present life.
Because the mind of the śramaṇa rejoices in emptiness and so forth, and because he practices the conduct of the transformation body for future births—
this is what should be known as the power of practice (*caryā-vega*). Because he relies on the practice of *tathatā*,

because his mind has faith in the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), because he does not delight in nirvāṇa, and because he does not delight in emptiness, he is also free from improper attachment to the provisional names and characteristics regarding both that which is to be attained and that which is capable of being attained.
"Always relying on the definitive meaning (nītārtha) and not on the literal expression" means that one seeks the intended meaning required for liberation;
rather than fleeing outward from within the afflictions (kleśa), one does not follow the nature of mere sounds.
This is what is called the "power of the mind," which should be understood as follows:

one perceives that the essence of all phenomena is eternally pure and unstained because of the nature of *tathatā* (suchness). Thus, one manifests forms for oneself and others; yet, this does not involve the cognitive nature of others, for it is a realization free from defilement.
Within this, all retributions and so forth are seen as entirely liberated, because one does not perceive the nature or characteristics of provisional names.
This should be understood as the power of realization.
Because the intrinsic nature of all sentient beings is extinguished, they do not engage in the cultivation of antidotes for all afflictions and defilements.
One does not grasp at extinction because True Suchness (tathatā) is uninterrupted, nor does one contemplate non-phenomena.
This is to be known as the power of reaching the ultimate exhaustion.

In this regard, the parable of the poor man should be understood as representing the śramaṇa who trains improperly; by way of three characteristics, he is known to be such that his name does not accord with its meaning.
There are those who destroy the mind while accomplishing conduct, those who accomplish the mind while destroying conduct, and those who both destroy the mind and destroy conduct.
Among these, one should know that there are three types of those who destroy the mind while accomplishing conduct.

They take contentment as their goal regarding both the ability to hear and that which is heard; they take contentment as their goal regarding the ability to explain those matters; and because they have attained worldly samādhi, they take delight in and become attached to those merits.

In this context, the metaphor of drifting and falling into a river explains the accomplishment of practice through a corrupted mind; one should know that it consists solely of matters such as hearing [the Dharma].
The metaphor of the physician likewise should be known to consist solely of matters of explanation.
The simile of the illusion should be understood as the attainment of worldly samādhi, wherein one merely delights in and clings to those phenomena.
The simile of the mani jewel should be understood as the perfection of the mind while the [former] conduct is abandoned.
The parable of death should be understood as referring to the corruption of mind and the corruption of conduct;
the parable of the householder’s son should be understood as referring to the perfection of mind and the perfection of conduct.
By means of this single characteristic, the well-trained śramaṇa should understand [these matters].
It is said that there are four kinds of precept-breaking bhikṣus who resemble those who properly maintain the precepts; what is their sequence?
By means of being a true śramaṇa, they manifest the undertaking of true practice.
To demonstrate that which resembles the precepts while abiding in conventional designations (prajñapti), one demonstrates the conventional designation of the precepts.
What is this demonstration of the conventional designation of the precepts?
It should be understood that there are four kinds of conduct for one who abides in the conventional designation of the precepts.
Furthermore, because they corrupt their bodies through pride and other such afflictions, they are said to abide in the practice of precepts that are merely nominal.
As for the former, they accomplish six kinds of precepts, yet their precepts are corrupted by two kinds of obstacles.
What constitutes the sixfold division of the training in the observance of the precepts?

It consists of: practicing according to what is taught in the Prātimokṣa; achieving success in practice; achieving success in conduct; achieving success in the mastery of objective spheres; perceiving fear even in minor transgressions; and undertaking and practicing [the training].
Regarding the various precepts, there are two kinds of obstacles.
What are these two? They are the intense proliferation of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which causes [transgressions] to arise within the precepts, and the concern for life.
Second, he abandons those two afflictions because he has departed from the state of the blazing view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
As a master of the Vinaya, he is well able to initiate [correct practice] regarding all transgressions of the precepts.
Nevertheless, because he is pure like the world, he cannot be moved by various gains and offerings, yet he remains identical to those who harbor the view of a self-identity.

Third, although they likewise attain the mundane pure precepts through this same Dharma, they further share with ordinary beings the view of a self-existent body; failing to understand the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), they experience terror and indolence upon hearing [the teaching].
The fourth is the abandonment of all faults; however, because one has faith in the false doctrine of non-self, one destroys the precept of pride and dwells in four kinds of improper precepts.
One should know that the perception of such dharmas as slander constitutes the precept, and its characteristic is to be understood as being untainted (*anāsrava*).
What are the dharmas of slander and so forth?
One who abides in the preliminary stage of the nominal precepts also perceives a self and speaks of "mine"; to counteract that, it is said that there is no self and nothing belonging to a self.
That which constitutes a transgression of the precepts is called "non-doing"; because it serves as the antidote to that, it is said that there is neither doing nor non-doing.
That which constitutes the practice of such actions is also not a practice; because it serves as the antidote to that, it is said that there is neither an action performed nor an agent.
Tranquil conduct is also called "non-conduct"; because it serves as the antidote to that [distraction], it is said that there is neither conduct nor non-conduct.
Conduct characterized by false mindfulness is called "non-conduct"; because it serves as the antidote to that, it is said that there is nothing that is conducted, nor anything that is not conducted.

The second dwelling is the practice of conventional precepts, which accords with the afflictions associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and also involves views regarding names and forms. To counteract these, it is said that there are "no names and no forms."
Regarding the perception of future birth and the perception of that [birth], in order to counteract them, it is said: "neither perception nor non-perception.
Regarding those who are intensely aflame with the afflictions (*kleśa*) yet are called "not extinguished," in order to counteract them, it is said: "neither extinction nor non-extinction."

Because it serves as an antidote to the grasping at a personal self and the grasping at what is to be accepted or rejected regarding persons, it is said that there is neither acceptance nor rejection.

Furthermore, because it serves as an antidote to the notion that within the very absence of a personal self in sentient beings there is both that which can be accepted and that which cannot be accepted, it is said that there is nothing to be accepted and nothing to be rejected.

One does not grasp at the marks of sentient beings by means of form and so forth; that is called grasping at "excellent. To counteract that, it is said: "There are no sentient beings, nor is there the name 'sentient being'.

Speech also describes that grasping at "excellent" through conceptualization; to counteract that, it is said: "There is no body, nor is there the name 'body'; there is no mouth, nor is there the name 'mouth'."
That which discriminates is the mind, and the grasping at that discrimination as "excellent" is its counteractive; therefore, it is said: "no mind, no mental discrimination.

For the practitioner of the third dwelling who observes the precepts, because they have transcended the world and are also directed toward relinquishing what is below, they are not of the world; to counteract that, it is said: "no world, no non-world."
Relying on samādhi and relying on non-attachment, because they serve as antidotes to those [faults], it is said: "There is no reliance, nor is there non-reliance.

Gathering one's own precepts and not disparaging the precepts of others, because they serve as antidotes to those [faults], it is said: "One does not exalt oneself through precepts, nor does one disparage the precepts of others."

The fourth dwelling is the precept of conventional designation; because one gives rise to discriminative thoughts, saying "I am one who can uphold the precepts," it is said that one must also not discriminate regarding the precepts, in order to counteract that [discrimination].

The discrimination of mindfulness regarding the superior nature and so forth is countered by non-discriminating precepts and the non-recollection of these precepts; therefore, this is called slandering the Dharma.
Within untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*), one is able to completely extinguish [all defilements]; this is called the phrase "the untainted fulfillment of the precepts maintained by the noble ones.
That which is "without attachment" is because it is supramundane; it does not reach the principle of the three realms and does not accord with any afflictions (*kleśa*).
Being free from all dependencies, it serves as the antidote for detachment from the three realms.
Therefore, regarding existence, there is a manifestation of supreme purity because of that person's observance of the precepts.
One should understand that these verses are spoken accordingly:
"One who is fully endowed with the observance of precepts is stainless and possesses nothing.
Regarding the first phrase of the initial verse, it is said that the nature is pure because it is free from defilement.

When greed and the other [afflictions] have been further abandoned, because their causes are purified, one attains the purity of the nature of morality; this demonstrates the equality of the purity of the cause.
As for the remaining three phrases, they refer back to that very observance of morality, demonstrating the equality of the purity of its associated causes.

In this regard, because of the counteraction of unvirtuous companions and their various common causes, one should understand that there are three types of distinctions among virtuous companions and their various common causes.

Among these, there are three kinds of companions who break the precepts: those who are equal in pride, those who are equal in appearance, and so forth. Because they rely on the same causes, because their minds are deluded, and because their views are like those of a fool, they share the same delight in *samāpatti* (meditative attainment); thus, through such association, they take up mindfulness.
Regarding "shared mindfulness" (*samānārthatā*): it is like deer dwelling together in a shared bodily pleasure, affection, and joyful companionship; this is the meaning of the first verse.
Furthermore, regarding all aspects within that very observance of precepts, one should know that the second verse is taught to clarify reliance upon pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Regarding such statements as "quiescence," "permanence," and "ultimate," one should know that within these there are four kinds of common afflictions; because they serve as their antidotes, the purity of the *pratimokṣa* precepts is taught, for they are not deficient.

Regarding the purity of the precepts through receiving them and the purity of meditative concentration, as well as the other purity of untainted (anāsrava) precepts, it is based on that very observance of the precepts—being pure and free from all afflictions—that the third verse is spoken.
"Not being stingy with one's body or life.
There are five such afflictions. What are those five afflictions?
First is the affliction of gain, honor, and respect, because of cherishing the body.
Second is the affliction of indolence, because one continues to dwell on the thought of not dying and gives rise to a fondness for life.
Third is the affliction of making vows to maintain the holy life, because of the longing for all forms of existence.
Fourth, there is the affliction of regarding the precepts alone as sufficient, because one does not arrive at what is correct.
Fifth, there is the affliction of failing to emerge [from suffering], because, like the various non-Buddhists, they propound doctrines that do not accord with correct principle.
One should understand that because these five kinds of afflictions are far removed, it is established that [the precepts] are pure and free from all afflictions.
Based on the purity of being without afflictions (*kleśa*), the fourth verse says:
"Holding the precepts, one is unstained by the world."
Because worldly dharmas cannot defile them.

Relying on the defilements subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), they equally arrive at the place where intense defilement arises and desire is produced; since the two consciousnesses are attached to various defiled cravings, it is said that they do not rely on worldly dharmas.
"Not relying on the world" means that because craving arises again after its cessation, it is extinguished.
"One swiftly attains the light of wisdom; by virtue of having attained this radiance, within the path of seeing the truths."
It is unimpeded and non-existent.
Regarding the state of being unimpeded and non-existent, it is said because one cultivates the path to counteract ignorance and other such factors.
It is selfless and devoid of those characteristics, for it is free from the notions of "self" and "other."
Because of the purity resulting from the abandonment of the conceit "I am" through the path of no-more-learning, the fifth verse says:
"There is no this shore, no other shore, And likewise, no middle."
In the practice of signlessness (*animitta*), one does not cling to the internal or external sense bases (*āyatana*).
It is without attachment or bondage and is untainted (*anāsrava*), because it extinguishes the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and brings about their total cessation.
It is without guile and is untainted, being free from the distinctions of the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*).
To clarify that [the mind] relies on eternal purity, the sixth verse states:
"The mind does not cling to name-and-form.
Because one does not give rise to aspirations for existence, one does not depart from the dharma of quiescence.
Because that person’s observance of the precepts was insufficient, because their faculties were not fully subdued, and because they lacked mastery within samādhi,
they did not give rise to the notions of "I" and "mine" even up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), for they were contented and remained steadfast in their ethical discipline.
It should be understood that the seventh verse is spoken in order to demonstrate that within the context of ethical discipline (*śīla*), one eternally manifests reliance upon worldly purity:
"Though practicing and upholding all precepts, his mind does not become conceited."
He manifests that because of upholding the precepts, the mind does not give rise to pride or arrogance, nor does it feel satiety;
thus, he does not regard this as supreme, but seeks the Noble Path beyond it.
Regarding those who purely maintain the precepts, because their meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is insufficient, they seek the supramundane path.
Relying on the purity of the supramundane, the eighth verse says:
"One does not take the precepts as supreme."
He does not take his stand on the precepts, because he does not consider them sufficient.
Nor does he prize meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
because he does not delight in or become attached to it.
"Having transcended these two matters, one cultivates supreme wisdom.
Non-conceptualization is the noble nature;
non-conceptualization is cultivation. It encompasses superior knowledge and is praised by all Buddhas."
Therefore, it is known that the others are superior because they praise the matter.
Based on the purity of those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those who are neither in training nor beyond training, the ninth verse says:
"The mind is liberated from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)."
"By extinguishing the conceptual view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), he demonstrates the purity of training in the precepts.
By eliminating 'I' and 'mine,' and by extinguishing the co-arisen view of a self-identity, he demonstrates the purity of the precepts of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)."
"Faith in emptiness is the realm of the Buddhas.
Because of faith in emptiness, there is the manifestation of pure phenomena that are neither of the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) nor beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Based on attachment to purity, the tenth verse is spoken:
"By relying on the precepts, one attains samādhi; through samādhi, one is able to cultivate wisdom.
This is said because it demonstrates that those who have not yet attained the precepts of the Eightfold Noble Path do not possess pure ethical discipline.
"By relying on the wisdom cultivated through causes, one swiftly attains pure gnosis;
because pure gnosis is attained, one becomes fully endowed with pure ethical discipline.
This verse was spoken to demonstrate that by attaining noble gnosis, one subsequently attains the purity of ethical discipline.
“At that time, eight hundred bhikṣus, through the non-clinging of all outflows, attained liberation of mind;

thirty-two thousand people were freed from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye. This demonstrates that within these instructions there are such great benefits, and it further shows that one attains the great fruit immediately, because those being converted—whether they be those still in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa)—attain it.

Regarding the statement, “And five hundred bhikṣus who had attained meditative concentration, upon hearing this profound Dharma, did not believe or understand it with their minds and were unable to penetrate it; they rose from their seats and departed,” this demonstrates that although those who were difficult to subdue had been subdued, they were nonetheless unable to believe or understand, and unable to penetrate and enter into the profound Dharma.
There are two characteristics that prevent one from penetrating all phenomena:
because of a lack of faith, and because, despite having faith, one does not delight in it; thus, wisdom cannot penetrate the various meanings.
This verse is profound because it is difficult to understand.
The bodhi of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is profound because its intent is difficult to fathom.

If one has not planted various roots of goodness with purity, is influenced by evil associates, and possesses little power of self-confidence, it will be difficult for such a person to gain faith and acceptance.
"Because they are influenced by evil associates, they do not purely cultivate the various roots of goodness; this should be understood as being due to a great deal of lack of faith.

At that time, the World-Honored One spoke to the Venerable Subhūti, revealing that at the time of awakening, all śrāvakas are created by the Tathāgata, for they are capable of transforming and delivering others through the ultimate truth.
Therefore, one should understand that there is a distinction between the provisional name and the ultimate reality.
As for the statement, "At that time, the World-Honored One immediately manifested two bhikṣus," it demonstrates the Tathāgata’s skillful means in responding to those who are to be saved.
Because there are two aspects to the manifestation of transformation: manifesting faith through wearing the same robes and seeing the same Dharma activities;
and because those bhikṣus are gathered in by being given correct instruction for themselves.

Because they grasp at nirvāṇa through false attachment and give rise to the conceit of "I," they experience fear; therefore, for the sake of their faith, it is said that in true nirvāṇa there are no sentient beings.
If one enters nirvāṇa, it is not because various things such as greed exist and then undergo extinction.
That [state] is like non-arising.
What is manifested as nirvāṇa is merely the cessation of arising.
When it says, "You should not form recollections or engage in discrimination," it refers to the notions of "I" and "mine" within the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*).
Respectively:
"Non-attachment to all phenomena" is because greed and hatred are fundamentally unarisen;
"non-detachment" is because they will not be separated from in the future.

This is called "one who is in cessation"; guarding against this attachment, although there is originally no cessation, there is cessation. As for all such categories as the precepts and so forth, they likewise neither abide nor come.
Furthermore, it is not extinguished because the name "sentient beings" is eternally quiescent.
It neither abides nor comes because it is undefiled.
Furthermore, it is not extinguished because its nature is itself extinction.
That [nirvana] is also not something remaining; if it were not originally quiescent and only later became quiescent, you should abandon such a notion.
This is because what is called nirvana is the absence of such things.
Do not say, "I shall enter nirvāṇa," for it is by means of signs that one is directed toward nirvāṇa, and thus one creates the sign of nirvāṇa.
Do not recognize the sign of nirvāṇa through signs such as desire; it is not because desire and the like are absent that it is called nirvāṇa. This is what is meant by "the sign of that."
Furthermore, regarding the skillful means within the practice of signlessness (*animitta*),

once the untainted (*anāsrava*) state has been established, the skillful means for the practice of happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) are subsequently explained, because one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and emerges from it.
Alternatively, this may have a different meaning.
When the Sūtra says, "If they do not purely plant various roots of goodness," it is because they lack the wisdom, merit, and practices that assist the path.
The phrase "the dust of predominant afflictions is not subsumed by unwholesome spiritual friends" means that it is not subsumed by wholesome spiritual friends.
The phrase "one who destroys this meaning cannot have faith and understanding" means that they are devoid of the practice of wisdom that aids the path.

Those who are able to believe in the profound realm but cannot believe and understand its meaning, and therefore cannot comprehensively penetrate it, are unable to fathom or know the wisdom that abides in the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, they are unable to believe or resolve it because they have not yet attained correct discernment through true wisdom.
It should be known that there are two kinds of skillful means by which the Tathāgata transforms and delivers beings:
first, because [the disciples] share the same substance as their own ego-conceit (*asmimāna*), he manifests himself as sharing in their common activities.

Because what is taught accords with the practice of the instruction, because one who receives the instruction possesses the cause for transcending the world, and because it is the skillful means of teaching the correct and pure doctrine;
furthermore, it should be understood that this consists of four types.
Because there is fear regarding both defilement and purity;
because it is taught in accordance with reality, it eliminates the causes of affliction;
and because it provides instruction regarding pure dharmas, it abandons the causes of fear.
Furthermore, because it provides instruction on the present life and reveals the skillful means for the practice of supreme bliss;
because this body still possesses the view of self, as one has personally realized it; and because it relies upon instructions that accord with emptiness amidst both purity and defilement.
To say, "I shall give rise to fear and defilement though innocent," because of such defilement,
this worldly activity is called the first sign. When it is said,
"You should not form recollections or conceptualizations," this indicates that there are two kinds of conventional designations (prajñapti-svabhāva) which serve as the causes of affliction (kleśa).

Because of the conceptualization of the affliction of prideful attachment, and because of the conceptualization that clings to those virtues as being superior to faults, this is called the second characteristic.
It should be understood that purity is briefly of two kinds:
first, the practice of the path of purity; [the second is the fruit of purity].
Second is the purity of nirvāṇa.
Because there are two kinds of characteristics within this, you should know that the practice of the pure path is the cause for overcoming fear. "O bhikṣus!..."
Regarding the statement, "All categories of precepts neither come nor go, nor are they extinguished," this is because they are reckoned as eternally pure within *tathatā*.
The former [section] explained that there is no establishment of either the conceptualization of afflictions or the conceptualization of being free from afflictions.

Having thus discriminated between the afflictions and the freedom from afflictions within the practice of the pure path, one gives rise to fear regarding that practice of the pure path because of two types of characteristics; it should be understood that one thus gives rise to fear toward the cause of pure nirvāṇa.
"You should abandon this notion, namely, the grasping at the notion that 'nirvāṇa is not different from the nature of conventional designations.
Do not follow after notions, nor do not follow after non-notions; this is called the notion of nirvāṇa being distinct, because one recalls and constructs it as a mental object."
Do not conceive of perception as something distinct;
do not conceive of the observation of names as something distinct—this is called the thought of inner tranquility.
Furthermore, do not observe perception with perception, for these two are without cause.
One should know that not giving rise to fear regarding nirvāṇa is called the third perception.
One should know that because those two causes have been abandoned, the various skillful means for the supreme practice are taught.
Abandoning those two causes of activity and abandoning the cause of afflictions, as well as abandoning the cause of fear within pure phenomena—this is what should be known as the fourth application.
Within this, one should understand the Tathāgata’s skillful means of transformation and deliverance.
From this point forward, it should be understood that correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) is explained as bringing about great benefit.
This is taught by way of six matters:
first, the matter of being a cause; [and so forth].
Second, the basis of phenomena;
third, the basis of resonant sounds;
fourth, the basis of tranquil contemplation.
Fifth, the matter of instruction;
sixth, the matter of realizing the Dharma and conforming to the Dharma.
It says: "At that time, the Venerable Subhūti asked those bhikṣus:"
"O bhikṣus! Where have you gone?
And from where have you come now?
The bhikṣus replied:
"Subhūti! The Dharma taught by the Buddha comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
For what reason is this said?
First, it is because they rely on the cause of pleasure.
For what reason is there no coming or going in that place?
It is analogous to the world.
He asked again, "Who is your teacher?
They replied, "Our teacher is that which has neither arisen in the past nor will it ever cease.
For what reason was this said?
Based on the second cause, because the World-Honored One is non-material and non-worldly, he is neither born nor extinguished, for he is of the nature of nirvāṇa.
[The Buddha] asked again: "What do you say?"
"From whom did you hear the Dharma?
He replied, "Neither for the sake of bondage, nor for the sake of liberation.
For what reason was this said?
The third [point] concerns teaching the Dharma based on the matter of the cause of echoes; it does not constitute bondage.
Because it serves as the antidote to the craving that arises from superior [conditions], it does not constitute liberation, for he has already attained liberation.
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, he asked: 'What dharma do you practice?
and they replied: 'Neither for the sake of extinguishing ignorance, nor for the sake of producing clarity'—what is the meaning of making such a statement?"
The fourth [reason] is because it relies on the contemplation of the object of tranquility; it is not for the sake of extinguishing ignorance (*avidyā*).
Nor is it because of relying on a confused ignorance, for the noble ones hear that those formations exist.
"One who does not bring about the arising of illumination" means that [illumination] has already arisen.
Again, he asked, "Who is your teacher?
They replied, "It is one who neither attains nor knows."
Regarding those disciples who have neither attained nor realized [the goal], for what reason is it said thus?
It is because of the fifth matter of instruction.
Since all the manifested bodies of monks are exhorted to them, one should know that the sixth matter—realizing the Dharma and practicing in accordance with the Dharma—is taught based on ten matters.

Based on *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, one extinguishes the afflictions associated with the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), extinguishes the afflictions associated with the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and extinguishes suffering; thereby making offerings to the Venerable One, practicing the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), transcending the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), entering and abiding in the stage of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*), and attaining liberation together with others.
When it is asked again, "Who are those with whom you practice the holy life (brahmacarya)?
and they reply, "Those who neither act within the three realms nor do not act," what is the meaning of making such a statement?
Because there is still something remaining in *nirvāṇa* without remainder, at that time they dwell together with those who share the same Dharma.
Again, he asked: "How long will it be before you attain *nirvāṇa*?"
The answer was: "If a person created by the Tathāgata were to enter parinirvāṇa, we too should likewise attain entry. For what purpose was this said?

Based on *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, because that [state] is the original arising and cessation, because it accords with the fundamental karma of similar phenomena through the power of others, and because at that time one dwells together with the remainder.
Regarding the statement, “He asked again, ‘Have your afflictions been exhausted?
and they replied, ‘All dharmas are ultimately characterized by exhaustion’”—with what meaning was this said?
Because the afflictions of the truths have been extinguished, all phenomena are eternally extinguished; that is, the various realms of existence and evil states are extinguished.
He asked again, "Have you all attained your own benefit?"
Regarding the response, "I know and have abandoned [the view of] no-self and what belongs to no-self," for what reason is this said?
It is because one relies on the cultivation of the perception of cessation to eliminate afflictions, and because one eliminates the co-arising view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the statement, "He asked again, 'Have you destroyed Māra?
and they replied, 'The skandha-māra cannot be apprehended,' what is the meaning for which such a saying was made?
It is because suffering has been extinguished, because the skandha-māra cannot be apprehended, and because future rebirth therein cannot be seen."
Therefore, one should know that within this, all demonic adversaries are subdued;
because the aggregates (*skandha*) do not exist, other demons do not prevail.
Again, he asked: "Do you all revere the Tathāgata?"
Regarding the reply, "Not by means of body, speech, or mind," for what reason is this said?
It is because one honors the Venerable One not through the body and so forth, but because one attains intimacy and reverence within the attainment of *nirvāṇa*.
He asked again, "Do you act as fields of merit?
They replied, "We take nothing, nor is there an agent.
For what reason was this said?
Because a donor’s act of reverence is neither to be accepted nor to be performed—since it is free from views, agitation, and evil—one asks in succession:
"Have you all severed the coming and going of birth and death?"
Regarding the response, "It is neither eternal nor annihilated," for what reason is this said?
It is because it transcends the stage of non-saints.
To prevent the world from falling into discontinuity by employing inferior, limited expedients—since there is indeed *nirvāṇa*—this demonstrates matters such as non-discontinuity.
Furthermore, when it is asked, "Do you practice in accordance with the stages of the noble ones?
and they reply, "We have abandoned all grasping and attained unimpeded liberation," what is the meaning intended by such a statement?
Because they abide in the stage of the noble ones, because they are liberated by being free from all grasping, and because they do not engage in arbitrary attachment or improper grasping.
[The Buddha] asked again: "Upon what, ultimately, do you rely?"
Regarding the response, "It follows wherever the emanated person of the Tathāgata goes," for what reason is this said?
It is because liberation is equally reached; since there is no distinct, superior, or dissimilar dharma in the Tathāgata, he manifests that liberation is equally reached.

Furthermore, those sons of good family who have attained mastery over the mind are able to receive the authentic prediction (vyākaraṇa) at the appropriate time; because they are such venerable ones, it should be understood that the subsequent bestowal of the authentic prediction will bring about great benefit.
What is the secret language?
It is the wisdom of non-dual characteristics,
as well as the entry into the characteristics of all secret languages as non-dual characteristics.

What are these? They are the phrases, locations, and entities that are spoken of; however, because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not exist, the nature of what is spoken of permeates a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*).
Since the nature and characteristics of the objective realm (*viṣaya*) exist [as such], they are non-dual.
He does not give rise to attachment toward non-duality; for dualistic characteristics are defiled, and because he does not grasp at duality, it is called "pure.

Although all that is spoken—every phrase and every locus—is said to have a referent, even those are merely conventional designations that perfume the signs, for the nature of their objective realm is non-existent.
Regarding the characteristics of those two types of perfuming: because the nature of their objects exists, there are those two.
