Because one clings to the characteristic of duality within that non-duality, there is defilement; because such clinging is exhausted, there is purity.
In this way, all Buddhas enter that secret language; it should be understood as the non-dual correspondence.

Regarding the five kinds of characteristics herein: within the venerable state and those instructions, there are five kinds of resultant matters and five kinds of beneficial resultant matters; because they accomplish and maintain these, one should understand that the various secret matters are taught.
There are five kinds of characteristics.
What are the five kinds of venerable ones?
If one has the perception that they are accomplished because of their speech, it should be known that this constitutes accomplishing the task of a venerable one.
Furthermore, what is its meaning?
It means that nirvāṇa is the eternal realization of that [reality].
The Dharma taught by the Buddha comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, for it is the cessation through the transcendence of the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
Because those who exist within that realm cannot be slandered by slanders, and because they are free from conceptual discrimination, one might ask:
among all phenomena, which is that Honored One capable of preaching the Dharma?
What are its characteristics?
It has never arisen from the beginning, nor does it undergo cessation, because the Dharma-body is without arising or cessation.
What kind of dharma is being taught?
If it is neither bondage nor liberation—
for the characteristics of both bondage and liberation do not exist—
then for the purpose of causing the awakening to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), by means of how many kinds of characteristics are they explained?
Because ignorance is neither extinguished nor does wisdom arise;
for the conventional nature of both wisdom and ignorance cannot be perceived or realized.
For whom was this taught?
If one has not yet attained [the fruit] and has not yet realized full awakening,
and because that [realization] does not cease until it is achieved,
what is the excellence of the result that is accomplished?
This refers to the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).

If one does not function within the three realms, but dwells in the locus of the realm of nirvana without remainder—which is the abode of pure *tathatā* alone—it is for this reason that the "nirvana with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*) is so designated.
If the Tathāgata is an emanation who enters the true state of *nirvāṇa*, there is only *prakṛti-nirvāṇa*.

All phenomena are said to be thus because they rely on *nirvāṇa* according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), for they are able to fulfill the practice of the Noble Path and have already accomplished what was to be done.

When it is said, "I have accomplished what was to be done," this is spoken based on the realization of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) regarding the notions of "self," "what belongs to the self," and "the self.

Because one has conquered internal enemies through internal power, and because one has eternally extinguished the enemies that are the various afflictions (*kleśa*) by realizing the selflessness of phenomena, such words are spoken.
One "subdues external enemies" because one does not perceive the demon of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*);
therefore, it should be understood that all that is comprised within the external aggregates is designated by the term "external enemy.
To "conquer them" means to be free from discursive conceptualization, for one does not perceive the intrinsic nature of the aggregates; this is how it should be understood.

Regarding the accomplishment of the fruits and beneficial matters therein: one has already paid reverence to the Honored One not merely through body and so forth, but by practicing the Dharma in accordance with it.

Because one has properly and purely received the offerings of the faithful, and because one understands the field of merit and does not grasp at any phenomena, one crosses over the ocean of suffering in the world.

Those who transcend the world do so because they realize the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), because they are free from the extremes of annihilation and permanence, and because they do not regress from the state of being a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
They traverse the ground of the field of merit by relinquishing the conceit of grasping and rejecting regarding phenomena.
Furthermore, those who are transformed by the Dharma are called "sons of the Buddha," because they rely upon the Tathāgata.
When it is said, "Where do you go when you practice? You go nowhere," this is because they come as those transformed by the Tathāgata.

Regarding the statement, "When Subhūti thus questioned and answered the bhikṣus, eight hundred bhikṣus attained liberation of mind through non-clinging to all phenomena, and thirty-two thousand people were freed from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye," this refers to the great beneficial events occurring within this very prophecy.
"If there are those in training who attain the stage of no-more-training, and ordinary beings who reach maturity and attain the stage of training"—"O Bhagavan!

This Dharma-door of Ratnakūṭa is rare; it can bring great benefit to sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna. From this point onward, the text reveals the matters of great benefit of this Dharma-door, because it is beneficial.

Regarding the factors for the enlightenment of bodhisattvas and the transformation of sentient beings, he provides instruction through the meaning of the Middle Way, and so forth, in successive order.

As for the question of how much merit those sons and daughters of good family obtain, this demonstrates that hearing the Bodhisattva-piṭaka brings about the benefit of faith through its instructional teachings.
"Kāśyapa! If there are sons or daughters of good family," and so forth—this demonstrates that there are five kinds of signs manifesting the benefit of the object of faith.
First, the greatness of the world's endurance during its period of stability;
Second, because of the cause for falling away from the attainment of mastery;
third, because of the transformation of the body;
fourth, because of that state, it is taught that one has attained the capacity to be a fit vessel.
The five types of listeners act as instruments for this purpose, and because they are able to perceive their pure karma at the time of casting off the body.
Among these, that which is "great" in the world refers to the Buddha, his śrāvakas, and all the stūpas and so forth.
Regarding "holding": it refers to filling all worlds with various jewels, robes, and so forth, because this lasts for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Within this, one should understand five characteristics that constitute the causes for the decline of great sovereignty:

(1) because there is a finite cause for the expectation of an infinite fruit; (2) because there is a distinction between exhaustible and inexhaustible phenomena; (3) because one has not attained the supreme bliss of the higher [stages]; (4) because they assist in knowing the nature of those practices; and (5) because they are drawn forth by them.
Furthermore, one should know that there are five kinds of characteristics that cause the attainment of the causes for the decline of great sovereignty (*maheśvara*):
first, because of attachment to even slight evil causes;
second, because of causes for pleasure that are not invariably constant.
Third, because it is not a cause for eternal happiness;
fourth, because it is a cause for experiencing pleasure through a perverted mind;
fifth, because it is a cause for experiencing pleasure based on a body of suffering—this is what is meant by "that."
Because one will finally receive a female body and then transform it, and because that place is revered like a sacred stūpa, that location serves as a vessel for practice.
Regarding those various dharmas that are read, recited, and upheld, the mention of "explaining" indicates that [the place] serves as a vessel for the speaker.

When those people reach the end of their lives, they are able to behold the Tathāgata; they attain purity of body, speech, and mental karma because they behold purity at the time of casting off the body.
Furthermore, because they attain pure karma, they are free from all afflictions, and thus, at the end of life, they are made to be separated from all painful sensations.
Furthermore, because he is free from the causes of sorrow and affliction, his mind cannot be overcome by sorrow and affliction.
He does not blink his eyes, for he knows with discerning awareness that all mental states exist.
He does not shake his hands or feet because he has perfected his dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).
He does not lose control of his excrement or urine, nor does perspiration appear on his chest, because he is free from fear.
He does not clench his fists or scratch at empty space, because he is devoid of all unwholesome characteristics.
He relinquishes his life as he sits because his body is thoroughly subdued;
his speech and voice are excellent and correct because he is free from all fears and difficulties;
his speech and voice are smooth and fluent because he is free from harsh and evil words.
"Exquisite speech and sound" refers to using sublime words to proclaim the wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
"Beloved speech and sound" refers to praising and speaking of all Tathāgatas.
Regarding "the speech and gentle tones that are joyfully protected by gods and humans": this is because those who share the same Dharma respond with reasoned answers.
Regarding "speech that is not contrary": this is because it is free from all falsehoods.
"Swift speech" means that the preceding and succeeding words do not contradict one another.
"Acceptable speech" means that it does not conflict with, but rather accords with, reason.
"Speech protected by devas" means that it is guarded by the various devas who have faith in the Buddha's Dharma.
Regarding the speech and sounds protected by all Buddhas: because they are taken into care by all Buddhas, they do not become angry and can immediately endure present evils.
Regarding their lack of resentment: they are able to endure past evils.
One who is not resentful does not conceal various evils.
One who harbors no intent for retaliation cannot be scorched by the heat of grief, regret, and the like.
One who does not calculate faults or calamities does not long for or seek after desire and its attachments.
"Not harboring" means not seeking to preserve [anything].
"Having no divergent characteristics and no timid mind regarding the precepts and dharmas" means not adopting divergent views.
"One who is always heedful and diligent in mind" means that their mind is not distracted and is tranquil.

"One who takes up the purity of the Buddha-world with a mind free from cowardice" means that they do not take pleasure in being sustained by themselves, but rather take up the most sublime Buddha-worlds through the support of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Those who are free from pride and overweening pride attain the manifest signs of all Buddha-dharmas.

Being free from pride and overweening pride, they do not seek out worldly samādhis and samāpattis through subtle and deep mental discrimination; rather, by using them as causes for the manifestation of all Buddha-dharmas, they do not regard them as superior.
The samādhis of all Buddhas constitute the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, through which one attains the benefit of correct faith and instruction.
One should know that such immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas, distinguished from their original differences, result in benefits of faith that become immeasurable, boundless, and asaṃkhyeya.
By the merit I have gained from composing this *Ratnakūṭa-śāstra*,
through the purity of my courageous resolve, may the world attain ultimate perfection.
This *Saddharmaratnakūṭa-sūtra* is the stainless light of great wisdom.
By the merit obtained from composing and transcribing this treatise, which removes the cataracts of obscuration,
may all those who cling to various views and have fallen into the net of ignorance quickly attain the unobstructed Buddha-eye in this world.
